en: The Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka: Prajāpati is indeed the year;
this Mahāvrata is his very self.
Therefore, one should not speak of this to another, lest one should place one's own self within another among all beings.
Moreover, this Mahāvrata is the very self of Indra;
therefore, one should not recite it to another, lest one should place the self of Indra within another.
Moreover, this Mahāvrata is the self of that very person whom they consecrate as consisting of the Ṛg, the Yajus, and the Sāman;
therefore, one should not recite it to another, lest one should place the self of all the meters into another.
However, if he so desires, the Hotṛ priest may recite it for the performers of the sacrificial session;
for his father, or for his teacher, or indeed for himself, that chant becomes his.
Thus, by means of himself, he brings the sacrifice to fulfillment.
Its Stoma is the twenty-fivefold;
for there are twenty-four half-months in a year, [and thus it serves] for the attainment of the year itself.
Now, Prajāpati is indeed the twenty-fivefold year.
Furthermore, the twenty-fourfold has already been established previously; this twenty-fivefold is its goal.
A bull dedicated to Indra and a goat dedicated to Prajāpati are to be offered.
This day indeed belongs to Indra;
and Indra is Prajāpati;
thus it is the form of Prajāpati.
Moreover, this bull is indeed the form of Indra among cattle.
For this [offering], the Ājya-śastra consists of twelve verses beginning with "tasya viśoviśo vo atithim.
There are indeed twelve months in a year; it is for the attainment of the year itself. In that [śastra], there are two meters: the Gāyatrī and the Anuṣṭubh.
He recites this hymn of twenty-five verses beginning with "The men [kindle] Agni with their thoughts from the two fire-sticks.
For the *stoma* is indeed twenty-fivefold;
that *śastra* is successful which corresponds to the *stoma*.
In that [sacrifice], there are indeed two meters, the Virāj and the Triṣṭubh;
these amount to four.
For this entire universe is a fourfold thing; it is for the attainment of this very whole.
The *praüga* is in the *traiṣṭubha* metre;
the *triṣṭubh* is indeed the metre of Indra.
In that he causes him to prosper by means of his own metre, [he acts rightly].

"kuvid aṅga namasā ye vṛdhāsaḥ"—this verse for Vāyu contains the words "great" (mahat) and "increasing" (vṛdhavat); for this day is indeed characterized by greatness. Following that, the next triplet for Indra and Vāyu, beginning with "yāvattaras tanvo yāvadojaḥ," possesses the form of the phrase "yāvannaraś cakṣasā dīdhyānāḥ."
"Up has risen your eye, O Varuṇa, of fair aspect"—this is the verse for Mitra and Varuṇa, with the form: "Sūrya goes forth, stretching out his body.

"Who will hear us? Which one among those worthy of sacrifice?"—this is the verse for the Aśvins, with the form: "whom the daughter of Sūrya chose. "How has he grown great? For which Hotṛ-priest?"—this is the verse for Indra, containing the words "great" and "grown."
This day is like the Mahāvrata.

"Who [will protect] us from the Vasus? Who will be our protectors?"—this is the Vaiśvadeva hymn, by way of the form: "O Varuṇa and Mitra, [you are] more powerful than a mortal. And "May Sarasvatī also be pleased with us"—this is the hymn to Sarasvant, by way of the form: "The auspicious one has opened wide the two doors of Order."
This *prauga-śastra* is indeed the *kadvat* [containing the word 'kad'], composed in the *triṣṭubh* metre, arranged in triplets, and belongs to Vāmadeva.
Vāmadeva is Prajāpati; thus, they fulfill all desires within Prajāpati himself.
Regarding this, they say: "The morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) should not be in the *triṣṭubh* metre."
It confuses the opening of the sacrifice for one who has prepared the meters;
it should rather be that which belongs to the *ekāha* (one-day rite).
For the *ekāha* is indeed the Brahman.
This day is Brahman;
by means of Brahman itself, he thus brings that Brahman to fulfillment.
"Come to us like a chariot for aid"—this is the introductory verse (*pratipad*) of the *marutvatīya* śastra;
"O Vasu, this pressed juice"—this is the following verse (*anucara*).
This very sequence is the constant arrangement for the one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*).

Regarding this, the Brāhmaṇa has been stated: "O singer, my [hymns] are not without fervor" (*asat su me jaritaḥ sābhivegaḥ*). Having first recited the Vāsukra hymn, he places the *nivid* within this Triṣṭubh verse: "Great is Indra, man-like, filling the people" (*mahāṁ indro nṛvad ā carṣaṇiprāḥ*).
As for why he recites the Vāsukra first:
Indra is indeed Vasukra; and as for [the verse] "Great Indra, manly, filling the people," it contains the word "great" (mahat),
for this day is indeed great.
Then he offers these oblations of clarified butter;
thereby he effects a blessing,
for the peace of the sacrifice and for the healing of the sacrificers.
There are eight of them; for by means of these, the gods attained all their desires. In the same way, the sacrificers also attain all their desires by means of these very [verses].
Then he mutters these *parimāda* prayers. Regarding the *parimādas*: water, indeed, is the *parimāda*; for by water all this [world] is measured out (*parimatta*).
Now, indeed, this is exhilaration; this *uktha* is food.
Water, being the source of food, comes first.
The waters are the *parimādas*. Now, the *parimādas* are indeed the nails, the teeth, the skin, and the body hair;
therefore, magical spells (*kṛtyās*) are always successful.
The *nidhana* consists of twenty-five syllables;
it has the form of the *āṅgirasa* for the sake of stability. This *bhūtacchandas* Sāman reached the beloved abode of Indra.
In *krośānukrośe*, they succeeded; in *apyeṣāṃ payaḥ*, they succeeded;
and [they offered] *arka* and *arkapuṣpa*.
This fire is the *arka*;
yonder sun is the *arkapuṣpa*.
When the chanters of the Sāmans praise them in succession, [they do so with these verses].
Then they say to the Hotṛ, "Recite after [the chant]. He should recite after them if they should chant;
whether they chant in this manner or if they should chant at all, he should simply recite after them.
These indeed are the seven meters of the gods;
therefore, one should recite them after [the main hymns].
Moreover, this day belongs to Indra.
The *japas* belong to Indra;
therefore, one should repeat them after him.
Then, standing right there, he pays homage to Agni limb by limb, saying, "Homage! Homage!"
For the gods do not surpass the act of salutation;
he should pay homage to these portions of the well-kindled fire if it is on the high altar (uttaravedi).
Then, standing right here, he pays homage to the sun.
"Let them make the space for the hall," so say some;
however, one should rather stand nearby, for he (Agni) speaks the highest blessings while remaining concealed within this supreme Uktha, saying: "The Great One has established himself in the great.
Agni is indeed the Great One, and this earth is the Great One.
For these two joined together with the words,
"May the god unite with the goddess";
Vāyu is indeed the god, and the intermediate space is the goddess.
For these two entered into union: "May the Brahman be united with the Brāhmaṇī.
That sun is the Brahman, and that sky is the Brāhmaṇī.
For these two joined them together; thus he joins these worlds together when he shall recite this *uktha*.
Viśvāmitra indeed approached the beloved abode of Indra through his recitation of the *śastra* and his observance of vows.
Indra said to him, "Viśvāmitra, choose a boon.
Viśvāmitra replied, "May I know you alone."
"The second" means "you yourself";
"the third" means [the same].
"Only you," [she said]. To him Indra replied: "I am great and I am the Great One;
I am the god and I am the Goddess."
"I am both Brahmā and a Brāhmaṇī.
Thereupon Viśvāmitra indeed desired to test him.
Indra said to him: "O Seer, that which I have spoken is indeed this; yet whatever is more than this, resulting from greater austerity—that alone would truly be what I am."
Indra then spoke those *vyāhṛti* formulas, saying, "They have been obtained. Then, having set down the swing-board, he anointed it three times and blew upon it three times.
Now, that [wood] is made of *udumbara*;

for the *udumbara* is vigor and food, so it is for the attainment of vigor and food. Then, having touched it with his chest and shifting it toward his right side, he mutters: "Thou art the *arka*; let the Vasus mount thee with the *gāyatrī* metre; they have mounted thee"—thus indeed he says this.

"I ascend after them for the sake of sovereignty"—for this very thing they call "sovereignty. Then, setting aside the next portion of himself, he mutters: "May the Rudras mount thee with the Triṣṭubh metre; they have mounted," by which he says, "they have indeed mounted thee."

"I ascend after them for the sake of self-sovereignty (*svārājya*)," he says. For self-sovereignty is indeed higher than kingship. Then, shifting his position toward the southern part of himself, he mutters: "May the Ādityas mount you with the *jagatī* metre; they have mounted you. Thus he speaks.

"I ascend after them for sovereignty," he says. Sovereignty (*sāmrājya*) is indeed superior, as it were, to self-sovereignty (*svārājya*). Then, surpassing the subsequent portion of himself, he mutters: "May all the gods mount thee with the *ānuṣṭubh* metre; they have mounted thee"—this is what he thereby declares.
"I ascend after them, attaining all desires," he says.
For the attainment of all desires is indeed the highest of all things.
Then, having stepped forward and drawn his two feet together, he places them upon the ground.
Indeed, he becomes more uplifted from this world;
therefore, when he establishes [the fire],
he becomes firmly established in this world, upon a firm foundation.
Regarding the non-falling [of the swing]:
then he says, "Three times he has breathed upon it, three times he has breathed down upon it.
Then, having placed his lap on the swing-board so that it is directed from south to north, he touches the swing-board from behind toward the front with his right forefinger.
"May Prajāpati mount you; may Vāyu swing you," [he says].
Indeed, it is Prajāpati who mounts this, and Vāyu who swings that which is living.
Then, having rubbed it three times, he says, "I have rubbed it three times."
Then, having grasped his two hands with the palms facing forward, he murmurs the following prayer.
Speech is united with breath, and I am united with breath;
sight is united with mind, and I am united with mind.
"May Prajāpati be united with the cattle; may I be united with the cattle"—thus he utters this very blessing.
"Thou art Suparṇa, Garutman"—Suparṇa is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa).
Thinking, "I shall speak a pleasing word," he speaks this very word when about to speak it, thinking, "It will accomplish much; I shall accomplish much.
For this speech is indeed one that accomplishes much;
for much does he accomplish who attains the *śastra* of this day.

"Thinking, 'She will do more than much,' and 'He will do more than much'—for this speech indeed intends to do more than much; and he who attains the *śastra* of this day will indeed do more than much.
Thinking, 'She will go to heaven,' and 'He will go to heaven'—for this speech indeed intends to go to heaven; and he who attains the *śastra* of this day will indeed go to heaven.
One should simply say, 'Intending to carry these sacrificers to heaven.'"
One should say of him whom one hates, "Not N.N., not N.N.
For as many [of his merits] as he shakes off from that divine state after having reflected upon them, so many indeed does he shake off.
Those two [merits] do not become available for enjoyment at all.
He thus overcomes that very [enemy];
having overcome him, he takes him into himself.
Indeed, this [breath] becomes Vāyu, the vital breath, and recites this Uktha.
He thus overcomes that very [obstacle];
having overcome it, he takes it into himself.
He who reaches the end of this day becomes one who is joined to the Guru;
for him, being thus joined to the Guru, his vital breath (prāṇa) is the Lord, provided it has not been defeated. It is that very [breath] which he thereby overcomes.
Having thus overcome it, he places it within himself.
Indeed, there is no piercing this deity with a poisoned arrow, nor with a sword, nor with an axe, nor with anything at all.
Therefore, whoever reviles one who knows this becomes the more evil person.
He who knows thus does not fall; for one who knows thus there is no falling away; for one who knows thus there is no falling away. //8//
Thus ends the first chapter of the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka.
One begins this *uktha* with the *hiṃkāra*.
The *hiṃkāra* is indeed breath; thus, one begins this *uktha* with breath.
Moreover, the *hiṃkāra* is vigor and sap; thus, he places vigor and sap into this *uktha*.
Moreover, the *hiṃkāra* is indeed immortality; he thus places immortality within himself.
The *rājana* is the *pṛṣṭha* chant.
The *rājana* is indeed the *sāman* that is manifest.
Thus he causes this very [sacrifice] to prosper by means of its own *sāman*.
That occurs over verses that are undefined (*anirukta*);
for Prajāpati is indeed undefined.
That is the form belonging to Prajāpati.
"It should be performed on the *kavatī* verses," so say some;
for Prajāpati is indeed *ka*.
That is the form belonging to Prajāpati.
Now he recites this *tūṣṇīṃśaṃsa* in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).
Speech indeed is this day, and the *tūṣṇīṃśaṃsa* is the mind.
By means of the mind alone, he brings that speech to fulfillment.
"That indeed was the eldest among beings"—this is the *stotriya* triplet.
"Increasing in power, possessing abundant strength"—thus it contains the word *vṛdha* (increasing) and the word *mahat* (great).
For this day is like the Mahad Uktha;
that is the twenty-fifth self. He recites that [hymn] as accompanied by the *nadana* sound.
The self is indeed the twenty-fifth; offspring and cattle are the *upasarga*. By means of offspring, cattle, servants, and food, he thus provides for himself.
With the words "Nadaṃ va odatīnām," he makes the preceding words *traiṣṭubha* and the subsequent ones *nada*.
With the first *triṣṭubh* foot, having placed the first footprint of the river together with the dawn, he pauses; with the second *triṣṭubh*, having joined the second together, he chants;
with the third *triṣṭubh*, having joined the third together, he pauses.
With the fourth [verse] in the *traiṣṭubha* meter, he joins and praises the fourth [verse].
Thus he recites the first [verse], expanded in this manner, three times; the subsequent [verses] are likewise expanded in this very way and are recited only once each.

He omits the second half-verse of the third hymn and also the second half-verse of the *nadasya* [hymn]. This is the opening of the mouth; through it he utters speech, for one indeed utters speech with the mouth.
He recites those two before the *dvipadās*; thus, having recited the self (*ātman*), his *stotriya* remains uninterrupted.
Now, the *sūdadohas* verses are the joints that hold [the hymns] together.
Furthermore, the *sūdadohas* is indeed water, for it is by means of water that these joints are held together.
Moreover, the *sūdadohas* is indeed immortality; thus, he bestows immortality upon himself.
Now, this *sūdadohas* verse is indeed the form of that [earth].
Just as there might be a resinous glue for wood or a leather-based adhesive, even so the eighty-three *ṛc*s of the *sūdadohas* serve as the binder for all the Vedas.
Then he recites these verses pertaining to the head;
they consist of three triplets,
for there are indeed three skull-bones in the head.
He joins those very [breaths] together by means of these [verses].
Those three [breaths] become one again, and that one becomes threefold, threefold; thus they become nine verses.
For there are indeed nine vital breaths in the head.
They contain the word "arka";
that is the characteristic form of this day.
Then he recites this "neck" (graiva) hymn.
These indeed consist of three verses;
for there are three joints in these necks.
He joins those very [joints] together with these [verses].
The *uṣṇih* is the last;
this is that shoulder-bone, split but not yet joined.
Then he recites this Akṣa hymn; it is indeed a Triṣṭubh verse,
and therefore the die is the largest.
"Lofty are your arms, O Indra, you the steadfast"—this is appropriate for the two arms.
Then he recites the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* verses of the *rathantara* [sāman].
Regarding these two, the Brāhmaṇa has already been explained.
Then he recites the *dhāyyā* verse. This earth, indeed, is the *dhāyyā*,
for she is established for the benefit of all beings.
She is indeed placed on the right side;
therefore, the woman lies upon the right side of the man.
Then he recites the *rāthantara* *pragātha*.
Regarding this, the Brāhmaṇa has been stated:

"He alone is indeed the one to whom the people bring oblations"—this hymn is to be recited verse by verse (*pacchas*). Having omitted its second verse with the words, "For every other has come as an enemy," [the rest is recited].
That which is its second [verse], he makes that the second here;
thus he interlocks these two wings so that they do not fall apart.
Then he recites this *prahastaka* verse;
these indeed consist of three *ṛc*s,
for there are three joints in his hand.
He joins those very [fingers] with these [verses].
The first is the Aticchandas; that is this thumb.
Therefore, this thumb reaches across all the fingers.
The right wing is the Rāthantara;
or rather, the left wing is the Bārhata.
By this very [statement], the Brāhmaṇa has been explained.
These two sides are the Bārhata and Rāthaṃtara, each consisting of twenty-four [verses];
for there are twenty-four half-months in a year, [thus it serves] for the attainment of the year.
Then he recites these [verses] in groups of four; that constitutes the *anūka*. These amount to twenty-one verses.
There are indeed twenty-one joints (*parvan*) in this *anūka*.
He joins those very [limbs] together with these [verses].
There are indeed seven triplets;
for there are seven meters, and it is for the attainment of all the meters.
They contain the word "arka";
that is the characteristic form of this day.
Then he recites these eighty verses;
by means of these, he recites in accordance with the *stotriyas*: the *gāyatra* by means of the *gāyatrī*, and the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* by means of the *auṣṇihī* and the *bārhatī*.
This very earth is the *gāyatrī* on the right side, the *auṣṇihī* on the left, and the *bārhatī* in the middle.
In the middle, this food is placed for oneself; between two *triṣṭubh* verses there is a *naividyā* verse. They belong to Viśvāmitra, contain the word "food" (*arka*), and are appropriate.
For Viśvāmitra saw this [hymn].
The opening verses contain words for "greatness" (mahadvat) and words for "increase" (vṛdhavat);
thus it is great and increasing.
"Like the Great One"—for this day is indeed like the Great One.

He begins the eighty-fold [stoma] with the *gāyatrī* verse, "Great is Indra, who by his might," using a verse containing the word "great" (*mahadvat*) and the word "increased" (*vṛdhavat*): "He has grown strong through the hymns of Vatsa.
It contains the word "great" and the word "increased";
it is "great" because this day is indeed great.

With the verse, "O Indra, bring those enjoyments," he enters upon the eighty verses in the Bṛhatī meter; with the verse containing the word "great" (*mahat*) and the word "increase" (*vṛdha*), namely, "O Maghavan, increase the singer of this [hymn].
It contains the word "great" and the word "increase.
It contains the word "great"—for this day is indeed great.

"May this be pleasing to you, O Indra, with your delightful bay horses, at the well-spoken hymn— namely, when he recites these at the end, thinking, 'May I ascend to the eighty verses of the *auṣṇiha* metre consisting of perfect *bṛhatī*s.'"

With the verse beginning "Indra, when the Soma-juices have been pressed," he enters upon this eighty-verse hymn in the *uṣṇih* metre: "He knows the increase of skill, for he is great"—this is with a verse containing the word *vṛdha* (increase) and the word *mahat* (great).
It contains *vṛdha* and *mahat*, for this day is indeed characterized by greatness (*mahadvat*).
These eighty verses, when recited together, amount to one hundred and twenty-seven ṛcs.

There are indeed seven hundred and twenty days and nights in a year; thus, by means of the eighty [verses], he obtains the days and nights of the year. Some, however, equate the Gāyatrīs with the Uṣṇih verses by means of the *nidhanas* of the Sāmans.
Some, however, take back the four-syllable units.

From the eighty Bārhata verses, he extracts eighty four-syllable units; from the Kākubha Pragāthas, twenty-four four-syllable units. These amount to four hundred four-syllable units, which he places into the four hundred Gāyatrīs.
In that way, those *gāyatrīs* become *uṣṇihs*;
one need not pay heed to this,
for it is already accomplished right here.
"Sing the Sāman for Indra!"—this is what he means when he recites this at the end: "May I ascend to the state of desire by means of the perfected Uṣṇih verses."
Then he recites the Vaśa hymn. The Vaśa is indeed the belly;
with that, once it has been successfully accomplished, one should desire to proceed without interruption.
Whatever [food] there is outside of this, he cooks that very thing for what is inside the belly.
Therefore, many deities and many meters are recited under control;
therefore, this manifold food of all forms is deposited within the belly.
Then these two half-verses are separated; then the *sūdadohas* verse;
that [verse] is then omitted from right there.
In this regard, the recitation is praised twenty-four times.
Then he recites these two-footed verses;
for the two-footed verse is a stable meter, and it serves for the sake of stability.
Then he recites this hymn to Indra and Agni consisting of Gāyatrī verses; for Indra and Agni are the two supports, and it serves for the sake of support.
Now he recites this Āvapana hymn;
for the Āvapana is a foundation, and it serves for the sake of stability.
Moreover, these very same verses become directed hitherward once again.
Then he recites this collection of verses in the *anuṣṭubh* meter.
This day is indeed speech, and the *anuṣṭubh* is speech; thus, he establishes speech upon speech.
With the words "Go to heaven," he goes to the gods by means of this hymn.
"Sa pratnathā kavivṛdhaḥ"—this triplet is rich in *arkas*; it is perfected by that [verse]. The last [verse] is a *gāyatrī*; it is perfected by that. "Śāsa itthā mahāṃ asi"—this is *mahadvat*.
For this day is indeed like the Mahāvrata.
Then he recites this hundred of Triṣṭubh verses. The Triṣṭubh is indeed the metre of Indra; thus he endows him with his own metre.
The *Hairaṇyastūpīya* and the *Yātaūtīya* belong to the Bṛhat and Rathantara; for the Bṛhat and Rathantara have already been performed previously.
"O Adhvaryus, bring the Soma for Indra," and so on; these constitute twenty-seven verses.
There are indeed twenty-seven lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*); thus, he attains the Virāj meter consisting of the lunar mansions.
One should recite that of Viśvāmitra,
for Viśvāmitra saw this.
One should recite that of Vāmadeva, for this is the "desirable" (*vāma*) of the gods.
One should recite the Vasiṣṭha hymn, for this belongs to the Vasiṣṭhas among the gods.
Therein, prior to the Udbrahmīya, he recites the word-appendages (anuṣaṅgas). Indeed, all desires are contained within this intermediate hymn (antaruktha).
Just as one would release cattle into a pen and then secure them with bolts and thorns,
even so, by means of these word-attachments (*padānuṣaṅga*), he grasps all desires on both sides and places them within himself.
Furthermore, the final verse belongs to the *Udbrahmīya* hymn and contains the word "arkavat" (possessing light).
That is the form of this day.
He concludes with a verse recited three times; having concluded, he mutters the *ukthavīrya*.
The one-day rite (*aikāhika*) comes first; it is indeed a foundation, and thus it serves for the sake of stability. The Mahāvrata rite comes later.
"Thou art great," he says; it contains the word "great," for this day indeed possesses greatness.

Thus, when the *sūdadohas* verse has been recited once, and as many verses as are included in the *upasarjanī* are being counted— excluding the silent recitation (*tūṣṇīṃśaṃsa*)— it results in a thousand *bṛhatī* verses.
Of this very thousand *bṛhatī* verses, there are thirty-six thousand syllables.
There are as many days in a hundred-year period;
he thus attains those days of a hundred-year period.
Some, however, say it is perfected by the *anuṣṭubh* meter.
Speech indeed is this day;
speech is the *anuṣṭubh*;
and speech, verily, is all beings.
"Or rather, speech is all this"—
thus it is established that [the sacrifice] is perfected by the Bṛhatī;
for he who shines yonder is indeed of the nature of the Bṛhatī.
Thus he causes him to prosper by means of his own metre;
he calls out three times,
for these worlds are three.
He attains these very worlds;
for the one-day sacrifice is a support, and it is for the sake of support that the one-day sacrifice is performed.
They loosen the swing even before the second *vaṣaṭ*-call has been uttered.
While still holding the cup, he descends; facing westward, he pushes away the swing-board.
While touching the cup, he mutters: "May I obtain that very prosperity which I have won. [He does this] lest he should exclude himself from that prosperity.
This is the Vaiśvakarman *atigrāhya* cup.
This day indeed belongs to Prajāpati;
Prajāpati is Viśvakarman, and thus he causes him (the sacrificer) to prosper through his own form.
And on this very day, Indra [bestowed it] upon Aṅgiras.
Aṅgiras spoke it to Dīrghatamas; from that, indeed, Dīrghatamas lived for ten human lifespans. Regarding this, the seer also said: "Dīrghatamas, the son of Mamatā, having grown old in the tenth age."
"Therefore, this is a weapon for one who desires long life," so said Kauṣītaki.
"He who, knowing thus, recites this day, attains a full lifespan in this world;
he obtains immortality and imperishability in the heavenly world."
"tat savitur vṛṇīmahe" is the opening verse (*pratipad*) of the Vaiśvadeva laud;
"vṛṇīmahe" contains the word *mahat* (great);
and this day is indeed characterized by the "Great" (*mahadvat*).
"O God Savitṛ, today for us... is the *anucara*; "May we meditate upon all desirable things" contains the word *mahat* (great), for this day is indeed connected with the *mahat*.
"The great desirable gift of the god Savitṛ"—this is the Sāvitra [verse], containing the word "great" (*mahadvat*);
for this day is indeed "great.

"For they two, Heaven and Earth, are the source of all prosperity"—this is the Dyāvāpṛthivīya [verse], containing the words "wide-extending," "magnificent," and "unfailing," thus it contains the word "great."
For this day is "great" (mahadvat);
thus [the verse] "What then, has the best, what the youngest come to us? belongs to the Ārbhava [Śastra].
And [the phrase] "We have not reviled the cup which is of great lineage" contains the word "great."
For this day is like the Mahāvrata; "Of this lovely, grey-haired Hotṛ" is the *salila* verse for the Viśvedevas,
for this [verse] is indeed the *salila* (the flowing) of the gods.
He places the *nivid* at the one-day sacrifice; for the one-day sacrifice is a foundation, and it is for the sake of stability. The *vaiśvānara* hymn belongs to the one-day sacrifice.
The one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*) is indeed a firm foundation; it serves for the sake of stability.
"The Maruts, eager to sacrifice, with glittering spears"—this is the verse addressed to the Maruts.
"Great, mighty, you rule far and wide"—this contains the word *bṛhat*.

"Like the Mahat"—this day is indeed like the Mahat. "Truly, it has been established among the works, made visible"—this is the Jātavedas hymn; its final verse contains the word "arkas": "Agni has been praised with powerful hymns. This is the characteristic form of this day, namely, the Agnimāruta hymns.
The hymns belong to this day;
thus the Agniṣṭoma is completed.
Indeed, the Agniṣṭoma is the Brahman.
This day is Brahman;
they establish Brahman in Brahman itself.
Those who undertake this day attain immortality—those who undertake this day.
Thus ends the second chapter of the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka.
Citra Gāṅgyāyani, being about to perform a sacrifice, chose Āruṇi [as his officiating priest].
He sent his son Śvetaketu, saying, "Go and conduct the sacrifice for him. When Śvetaketu had arrived, Citra questioned him: "O son of Gotama..."
"There exists a conventional path in the world in which you shall not be established;
or rather, there is another path in the world in which you shall not be established."
He said, "I do not know this; come, let me ask my teacher. Having approached his father, he asked him, "Thus has he questioned me; how shall I answer?
He replied, "I too do not know this."
"Only when we have completed our private Vedic study do we take what others give us.
Come, let us both go," he said.
Then, with fuel in his hand, he approached Citra Gāṅgyāyani, saying, "I come to you as a pupil."
He said to him: "O Gautama, you are worthy of Brahman, since you have not fallen into pride;
come, I shall indeed instruct you further."
He said: "Indeed, whoever departs from this world, they all go to the moon.
By their vital breaths, the waxing fortnight is nourished; by the waning fortnight, he causes them to be born again."
The moon is indeed the door to the heavenly world;
he who answers it is released [to go there],
but he who does not answer it becomes rain here and rains down upon this earth.

Whether he is born here as a worm, a moth, a fish, a bird, a lion, a boar, a dog, a tiger, a human, or some other being, he is reborn in those various places according to his karma and according to his knowledge. When he has arrived, [the teacher] asks him: "Who are you?"
He should reply to him: "From the discerning one, from the fifteenfold procreative father who possesses the ancestral heritage, the seed has been brought forth.
Impel that toward me as the male agent; through the male agent, pour it into me, the mother."
Being born, being reborn, with twelve or thirteen months;
with a father of twelve or thirteen, I have found that, I have truly found that. O Seasons, you who are immortal, take hold of me!
"By that truth, by that austerity, I am the season, I am the seasonal one.
To him who says, "Who are you? I am [so-and-so]," he grants permission to depart.
Having entered upon this path of the gods, he comes to the world of Agni;
thence to the world of Vāyu;
thence to the world of Varuṇa.
He [attains] the world of Indra;
he [attains] the world of Prajāpati;
he [attains] the world of Brahman.
Of this very world of Brahman,
the muhūrtas are the stair-ascenders, the yaṣṭihās are the pillars, and the Vijarā is the river.
That tree is the Sālajya, its configuration is the Sālajya,
and its abode is Aparājita.
Indra and Prajāpati are the door-keepers; Vibhu is the measured space;
Vicakṣaṇā is the throne.
Amitaujas was Paryaṅka,
Priyā was Mānasī,
and Pratirūpā was Cākṣuṣī.
Taking flowers,
they indeed weave the worlds, as well as the Apsarases Ambā and Ambāyavī,
and the rivers Ambayā.
One who knows this comes toward him.
Brahmā says to him: "Run toward me with my glory!
Or else, he has reached the river Vijarā."
"Or rather, he will not grow old."
Five hundred apsarases approach him: one hundred with fruits in their hands,
one hundred with ointments in their hands,
and one hundred with garlands in their hands.
There were a hundred women with garments in their hands and a hundred women with jewels in their hands;
they adorned him with the ornaments of Brahmā.
Adorned with the ornament of Brahman, knowing Brahman, he proceeds toward Brahman.
He comes to the pool Āraṃ and crosses over it by means of the mind.
Having struck him, those who possess full knowledge sink down;
he returns in a moment as the club-slayers,
and they flee from him.
He approaches the river Vijarā;
he crosses it by means of the mind alone,
whereby his good and evil deeds are shaken off.
His dear kinsmen take upon themselves his good deeds, and those who are not dear take upon themselves his evil deeds;
just as one driving a chariot would look down at the two wheels of the chariot as they revolve.
Thus one should examine day and night;
thus [one examines] good deeds and evil deeds, and all pairs of opposites. Such a person, having cast off both good and evil deeds, knowing Brahman, proceeds toward Brahman alone.
He comes to the Ilya tree;
the fragrance of Brahman enters him.
He comes to the Sālajya assembly hall.
The essence of Brahman enters him;
he arrives at the unconquerable abode;
the glory of Brahman enters him.
He calls out to Indra and Prajāpati, the gatekeepers;
they flee from him. He comes to Vibhu Pramita.
He enters that splendor of Brahman.
He approaches the Vicakṣaṇā throne;
the Bṛhat and Rathantara Sāmans are its two front feet.
The other two [stomas] are the Śyaita and Naudhasa; the Vairūpa and Vairāja are the Anūcya;
the Śākvara and Raivata are the Tiraścī.
That is wisdom, for by means of wisdom one sees clearly; he comes to the cross-legged posture of immeasurable power;
that is the vital breath (prāṇa).
Its two front feet are the past and the future;
its two hind feet are Śrī and Irā; and its two head-feet are the Bhadra and Yajñāyajñīya chants.
The Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans] are the two side-posts;
the Ṛg-verses and Sāman-chants are the longitudinal threads,
and the Yajus-formulas are the transverse threads.
The rays of the moon are the under-layer;
the Udgītha is the pillow;
and Śrī is the cushion.
Brahmā resides in that [world].
One who knows this ascends to its very summit by means of his foot alone.
Brahmā questions him.
"Who are you?"—
to him he should reply.
I am the season; I am the seasonal product.
Born from space as the womb, I am the seed for the wife; I am the self of the year, which has become the radiance of all that exists.
"You are the self of every being;
who you are, that am I. He said to him: "Who am I?"
One should say, "It is truth.
"What is that which is truth? "That which is other than the gods and the vital breaths—that is the real (sat)."
Now, that which consists of the gods and the vital breaths—that is the Real (satya).
That is expressed by a single word: "the True" (satyam).
This whole world is just this much.
"This is all I am"—this is what he says to him. This very point has been expressed in a verse:
He whose belly is the Yajur Veda, whose head is the Sāma Veda, whose form is the Ṛg Veda, and who is imperishable—
he is to be known as Brahman, the great seer composed of Brahman.
Thus it is said: "By what do you obtain my masculine names? He should reply, "By the vital breath (prāṇa)."
"By what are they called neuter?
"By the mind. "By what are they called feminine names?"
He says: "By what [does one perceive] odors?
"By the nose."
"By what [does one perceive] forms?
"By the eye.
"By what [does one perceive] sounds?"
"By what [does one perceive] sounds? "By the ear.
"By what [does one perceive] the flavors of food? "By the tongue."
"By what are actions performed?
"By the two hands.
"By what are pleasure and pain experienced?"
"By means of what body,
Ānanda, does one experience delight and procreation?
"By means of the organ of generation."
"By what [are] the breaths?
"By the two feet.
"By what [is] that which is to be known, the intellect, and the desires?"
"One should say, 'By wisdom alone.
He said to him: "This world of mine is indeed water; that [world] of yours is that.
That which is the victory of Brahman, that which is its individual manifestation—
He who knows thus wins that victory; he who knows thus attains that distinction—yea, he who knows thus.
Thus ends the third chapter in the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka.
"Breath is Brahman," so indeed said Kauṣītaki.
Of this very breath that is Brahman, the mind is the messenger,
and the eye is the guardian.
The ear is the one who causes to hear, and speech is the server. Indeed, he who knows the mind to be the messenger of this Brahman that is Prāṇa becomes possessed of a messenger.
He who is the protector of the eye becomes possessed of a protector;
he who is the one who causes hearing becomes possessed of one who causes thorough hearing;
he who is the enveloper of speech becomes possessed of an enveloper.
To this very Brahman, these deities bring tribute even though he does not ask for it;
in the same way, all beings bring tribute to him who knows this, even though he does not ask for it.
His secret doctrine (upaniṣad) is: "One should not beg."

It is just as if one were to go begging for alms in a village and, having received nothing, were to sit down thinking, "I shall not eat what has been given from here. Then those very people who previously refused him would invite him; such is the rule for one who does not beg.
But those who give food invite him, saying, "We shall give to you."
"Breath is Brahman," so Paiṅgya used to say. Of this very breath that is Brahman, speech extends beyond it; sight extends beyond that; and hearing extends beyond that.
The ear holds fast to the mind as superior;
the vital breath holds fast to the mind as superior.
To this very vital breath, the Brahman, these deities bring tribute without being asked.
In this very way, all beings bring tribute to one who knows this, even though he does not ask for it. His secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) is: "One should not beg.
It is just as if, having begged through a village and received nothing, one were to sit down and think, "I will not eat what has been given from here."
Those who previously refused him now invite him;
this is the rule for one who does not beg.
But those who give food indeed invite him, saying, "We shall give to you."
Now, therefore, follows the acquisition of a single prize (*ekadhana*).
One who desires to acquire a single prize should, on the full moon day, or the new moon day, or during the bright fortnight, or under an auspicious lunar mansion—
on one of these festival days— having established the fire, swept around it, strewn grass around it, and sprinkled water around it, [he should proceed] toward the south...
Having recited the invitatory formula, he offers the oblations with the *sruva* spoon:
"The deity named Speech is a bestower of acquisitions; may she bestow this upon me from that person; *svāhā* to her!
The deity named Breath is a bestower of acquisitions; may she bestow this upon me from that person; *svāhā* to her!"
The deity named Hearing, who bestows boons—may she grant this to me from that [source]; to her, svāhā!

The deity named Mind, who bestows boons—may she grant this to me from that [source]; to her, svāhā! The deity named Wisdom, who bestows boons—may she grant this to me from that [source]; to her, svāhā!

Then, having smelled the fragrance of smoke and having anointed his limbs with an offering of clarified butter, he should set out while restraining his speech and either state his purpose himself or dispatch a messenger;
he will surely obtain it.
Now, therefore, follows the divine *smara* (the rite for winning over memory).

For one whom he wishes to become dear—whether it be a man, a woman, or many people—he offers these oblations of clarified butter at one of their festival days (*parvan*), following this same procedure:
"I offer your speech into me, O [Name], svāhā!"
I offer your breath into me, O [Name], svāhā!
I offer your sight into me, O [Name], svāhā! I offer your hearing into me, O [Name], svāhā!
"I offer your mind into me, so-and-so, svāhā! I offer your wisdom into me, so-and-so, svāhā!
Then, having smelled the fragrance of the smoke and having anointed his limbs with the application of clarified butter, he should go forth silently, desiring to enter into physical contact.
Or he may stand while greeting him;
thus he becomes truly dear and is indeed remembered by him.
Now, therefore, follows the Sāṃyamana Prātardana sacrifice;
they call it the internal Agnihotra.
For as long as a person speaks, he is not able to breathe.
Then one offers the vital breath into speech;
for as long as a person breathes, he is not able to speak.
Then one offers speech into the vital breath.
These two offerings, which are infinite and immortal, he offers continuously while both waking and sleeping.
Now, as for other offerings, they are finite because they consist of ritual action (*karman*).
Therefore, the wise of old did not offer the *agnihotra* at all.
"Uktha is Brahman," so indeed said Śuṣkabhr̥ṅgāra. One should meditate upon that as the *Ṛc*.
Indeed, all beings will exalt him for his preeminence.
One should meditate upon that as the *yajus*;
for all beings are then yoked for his preeminence.
One should meditate upon that as the *sāman*.
All beings indeed bow down to him for his preeminence. One should meditate upon that as "Prosperity" (Śrī); one should meditate upon that as "Fame" (Yaśas).
One should worship that as "splendor.
Just as this [word] occurs among the Vedic hymns as the most glorious, the most renowned, and the most splendid,
even so does he who knows this become the most glorious, the most renowned, and the most splendid among all beings.
This very sacrificial rite pertaining to the iṣṭi is that self which the Adhvaryu prepares; therein he weaves the one consisting of the Yajus, and upon that which consists of the Yajus,
the Hotṛ weaves the one consisting of the Ṛc.
The Udgātṛ priest consists of the Sāman within that which consists of the Ṛc;
he is the self of the threefold knowledge.
And he who knows this becomes the very self of Indra.
Now, therefore, there are three forms of worship belonging to Sarvajit Kauṣītaki.
Sarvajit Kauṣītaki used to worship the rising sun: having arranged his sacred thread over the shoulder and brought water, he would pour it out three times into a water-vessel, saying:
"Thou art a separator; separate evil from me."
With this same procedure, he addresses him as he stands in the middle:
"Thou art the up-raiser; raise me up from evil.
With this same procedure, he addresses him as he goes westward.
"You are the gatherer; gather my evil away.
Whatever evil he does by day and night, he gathers that away.
And so, one who knows this likewise worships the sun with this very procedure.
Whatever evil one commits by day and night, that he removes.
Then, when the new moon has passed month after month, one should worship the moon as it becomes visible again, following this same procedure.

Or, having thrown green grass [into the fire], [one should recite]: "My heart with its beautiful border, which rests in the moon in heaven—I consider myself to know that; may I not weep over the calamity of losing a son."
Thus [it is said].
For it is not the case that offspring have already passed away before this [rite]; this is for one who has a son born.
Now, for one whose son is not yet born: "May you swell; may [the waters] gather unto you."

Having recited these three verses—"May thy juices come together, and may thy strengths come together; O Ādityas, that stalk which you cause to swell"—he says: "Do not cause me to swell with breath, progeny, or cattle; rather, cause him to swell with breath, progeny, and cattle who hates us and whom we hate. Then he turns toward the north with the verse addressed to Indra: "I turn toward the turning of Indra; I turn following the turning of the Sun," and [he turns] to the south.
It turns along the arm.
Then, on the full moon day, he should worship the moon as it becomes visible in the east, following this same procedure:
"O King Soma, you are far-seeing; you have five faces; you are Prajāpati. The Brahmin is one of your faces; with that face, you eat the king."
By that mouth, make me an eater of food.
You, O King, have one mouth; by that mouth you eat the subjects. By that mouth, make me an eater of food.
The hawk is one of your mouths; with that mouth you eat birds. With that mouth, make me an eater of food.
Fire is one of your mouths; with that mouth you eat this world.
"By that mouth, make me an eater of food;
do not diminish us in life, progeny, or cattle.
He who hates us and whom we hate—by his life, progeny, and cattle, may you diminish! Having said this, he turns toward the right, following the divine course, the course of the sun.
It turns along the arm.

Then, about to depart, he should touch his wife's heart, saying: "O woman with beautiful hair-parting, that heart of yours which rests within Prajāpati—by means of that, O mistress of immortality, may you not fall into the sin of childlessness."
For her offspring does not perish before its time.
Then, having returned from his journey, he should kiss his son's head, saying: "From limb by limb you are produced; from the heart you are born.
You are indeed the self (ātman) named 'son'; live for a hundred autumns! He then gives him a name, saying: "Be a stone! Be an axe!"
"Be invincible gold!
You are indeed the splendor of sons; live for a hundred autumns!"—with these words he takes his name.
Then he embraces him.
"With that by which Prajāpati encompassed his offspring, for safety, with this I encompass you, O [Name]!
Then he murmurs into his right ear: "O Maghavan, O drinker of the dregs, bestow upon us!
And into his left ear: "O Indra, bestow upon us the most excellent riches!"
"Do not fear, do not tremble; live for a hundred autumns of life!
O son, I smell your head with my name," saying this, he should smell his head three times.
"With the *hiṃkāra* of the cows, I *hiṃ* you," saying this, he makes the *hiṃkāra* over his head three times.
Now, therefore, follows the divine *parimara*. This Brahman indeed shines when the fire blazes; it dies when it does not blaze.
His radiance goes to the sun, and his vital breath to the wind.
Indeed, this Brahman shines when the sun is seen;
then it dies when it is no longer seen.
His radiance goes to the moon, and his breath to the wind.
This Brahman indeed shines when the moon is seen;
it dies when it is not seen.
His brilliance goes to lightning, and his vital breath to the wind.
Indeed, that which flashes as lightning is Brahman shining;
and when it does not flash, it dies.
Its radiance goes to fire, and its vital breath to the wind.
Indeed, all these deities, having entered the wind and having died in the wind, do not perish; from that very source they arise again.
Thus with reference to the divine;
now with reference to the self.
This Brahman indeed shines when one speaks with speech;
then it dies when one does not speak.
Its brilliance departs into the eye alone.
The vital breath is the vital breath.
Indeed, this Brahman shines when one sees with the eye;
but it dies when one does not see.
His sense of hearing indeed goes to its brilliance, and his breath to its breath. Verily,
that Brahman shines when one hears with the ear.
Now, when one dies such that one does not hear,
his mental faculty (*manas*) alone goes to its radiance (*tejas*),
and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) goes to the vital breath.
This Brahman indeed shines when one meditates upon it with the mind;
then it dies when one does not meditate upon it.
Its vital breath alone goes to its radiance.
The vital breath is the vital breath.
Indeed, all these deities, having entered into the vital breath alone and having merged into the vital breath, do not perish;
therefore, they emerge from it once again.
Therefore, if both mountains—the southern and the northern—should roll toward one who knows this here, even though they seek to crush him, they would not strike him down.
Rather, those who hate him and those whom he himself hates are the ones who perish around him.
Now, therefore, follows the attainment of the supreme good.
Indeed, these deities, contending for superiority among themselves, departed from this body;
then it fell down.
It lay there dry, having become like a piece of wood. Then speech entered it; yet even as it spoke with speech, it continued to lie there.
Then the eye entered it;
speaking with speech and seeing with the eye, it remained as if asleep.
Then the ear entered it.
It spoke with speech, saw with the eye, and heard with the ear, yet it remained as if lifeless.
Then the mind entered it;
it spoke with speech, saw with the eye, heard with the ear, and thought with the mind, yet it remained as if lifeless.

Then Prāṇa entered it, and it rose up from that very place. Indeed, all these deities, having recognized the superiority in Prāṇa and having merged into Prāṇa as the conscious self (prajñātman), departed together with all of them from this body.
They, having the wind as their support and space as their self, go to the heavenly world.

In the very same way, one who knows this, having understood the supreme good to reside in breath, and having fully realized the breath as the conscious self (*prajñātman*), departs from this body together with all these [elements].
Having the wind as his support and space as his self, he goes to the heavenly world.
He goes to where those gods are;
having reached that which the gods have attained as immortality,
he who knows thus becomes immortal.
Now, therefore, they explain the "Transmission from Father to Son.
When the father is about to depart for the next world, he calls his son.
Having strewn the house with fresh grass, kindled the fire, and placed a water-pot together with a vessel nearby, the father lies down covered by an unwashed garment.
Having approached, O son, sit down above him, touching his sense-faculties with your own sense-faculties;
or rather, he should hand it over while you are seated and facing him.
Then he hands it to him.
"May I place my speech in you," says the father. "I place your speech in myself," says the son.
"May I place my breath in you," says the father.
"Place your breath in me," says the son.
"I shall place my sight in you," says the father.
"Place your sight in me," says the son.
"May I place my hearing in you," says the father.
"May I place my hearing in you," says the son.
"May I place the essences of food in you," says the father.
"May I place the essence of food within you," says the son;
"May I place my actions within you," says the father; "May I place your actions within me," says the son.
"May I place my pleasure and pain in you," says the father; "May I place your pleasure and pain in me," says the son;
"May I place my joy, delight, and progeny in you," says the father.
"Joy, delight, and progeny—place these in me," says the son. "May I place vitality in you," says the father.
"Place vitality in me," says the son.
"May I place my thoughts, objects of knowledge, and desires in you," says the father.
"I place my thoughts, objects of knowledge, and desires in you," says the son. "May I place my mind in you," says the father.
"Place your mind in me," says the son;
"I shall place my wisdom in you," says the father;
"I place your wisdom in me," says the son.
Or, if he should be one who speaks in whispers, he should say it briefly:
"I place my vital breaths in you," says the father;
"I place your vital breaths in me."
The son, having turned to the right, steps out;
the father addresses him with the mantra:
"May glory, spiritual luster, and fame attend you."
Then the other looks toward the left shoulder, having covered [the boy] with his hand or with the edge of his garment, saying: "May you attain the heavenly worlds and all desires.
If he should be long-lived, the father may live under the sovereignty of his son.
Or he may go around it.
But if he should die, they should complete him in that very same way;
in whatever manner he is to be completed, in that manner he is to be completed.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka.
Pratardana, the son of Divodāsa, indeed approached the beloved abode of Indra through both battle and manly prowess.
Indra said to him, "Pratardana, choose a boon.
Pratardana replied, "Choose for me yourself that which you consider most beneficial for a human being."
Indra said to him: "One does not choose a boon for an inferior;
you yourself must choose.
Pratardana replied: "It is indeed said that I am inferior."
Then indeed Indra departed from truth alone, for Indra is truth.
Indra said to him: "Know me alone."
This indeed I consider most beneficial for a human being: that he should know me—
how I slew the three-headed son of Tvaṣṭṛ,
and how I delivered the Arumukhas and the Yatīs to the jackals.
Transgressing many covenants, I struck down the sons of Prahlāda in heaven, the Paulomas in the intermediate space, and the Kālakhañjas on earth;
yet not even a single hair of mine was harmed therein.
Whoever knows me—for him, indeed, no world is destroyed by any action whatsoever:
not by theft, not by the killing of an embryo, not by the murder of a mother, nor by the murder of a father; even for one who has committed sin today, the dark hue does not depart from his face.
He said: "I am the vital breath, the conscious self.
Meditate upon me as life and immortality. Life is the vital breath."
Life-breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed life (*āyus*).
As long as the life-breath remains in this body, so long does life exist.
For it is by means of the life-breath alone that one attains immortality in this world.
Through wisdom, one attains true resolve.
He who worships me as life and immortality reaches a full span of life in this world.
One attains immortality and imperishability in the heavenly world.
Regarding this, some say that the vital breaths (prāṇas) indeed become unified;
for no one would be able to simultaneously designate a name with speech, perceive a form with the eye, hear a sound with the ear, or contemplate with the mind.
"Indeed, having become one, these vital breaths (prāṇas) cause each one of them to perceive all things.
When speech speaks, all the vital breaths speak after it;
when the eye sees, all the vital breaths see after it."
When the ear hears, all the vital breaths hear after it;
when the mind thinks, all the vital breaths think after it;
when the vital breath breathes, all the vital breaths breathe after it.
"So indeed it is," said Indra;
"but there is indeed a higher good regarding the vital breaths."
One lives even when deprived of speech,
for we see those who are mute;
one lives even when deprived of sight.
For we see [others] who are [still] alive though deprived of hearing; for we see those who are deaf.
One lives even when deprived of the mind; indeed,
we see fools who live even with their arms cut off.
"One whose thighs have been cut off still lives"—
for we observe this to be so.
Now, it is indeed *prāṇa*, whose self is wisdom (*prajñātman*), that, having taken hold of this body, causes it to rise up.
Therefore, one should venerate this very Uktha.
This is the attainment of all things in the vital breath (prāṇa).
That which is the vital breath is indeed wisdom (prajñā).
Or rather, that which is wisdom is the vital breath;
this is its vision,
this is its consciousness.
When a person here is asleep and sees no dream at all,
then he becomes one with this very breath alone;
then speech enters into him together with all names.
The eye merges with all forms; the ear merges with all sounds;
the mind merges with all meditations.
When he awakens,
just as sparks fly out in all directions from a blazing fire, even so do the vital breaths (prāṇas) disperse from this Self according to their respective locations.
From the vital breaths come the gods;
from the gods, the worlds.
This very vital breath, being the self of intelligence, having taken hold of this body, causes it to rise up.
Therefore, one should venerate this very *uktha*.
This is the attainment of all things in the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Indeed, that which is the vital breath is wisdom (*prajñā*).
Or rather, that which is wisdom is breath;
this is its accomplishment;
this is the realization thereof.
When a person, being afflicted and about to die, having fallen into weakness, enters into a state of delusion, they say of him: "The mind has departed;
he does not hear."
He does not see;
he does not speak with speech; he does not contemplate.
Then, when this breath becomes one with each [of the senses],
speech enters into it together with all names;
the eye enters into it together with all forms.
The ear merges with all sounds; the mind merges with all thoughts. When he departs from this body, he departs together with all of these.
In him, all names are emitted through speech;
by means of speech, he attains all names. In him, all odors are emitted through the vital breath (prāṇa).
Through the vital breath (prāṇa), one obtains all odors;
through the eye alone, all forms are projected upon this [person];
and through the eye, one obtains all forms.
Into the ear alone all sounds are emitted;
through the ear one attains all sounds.
Into the mind alone all objects of thought are emitted.
Through the mind one obtains all things that have been meditated upon;
for these two dwell together in this body and depart together from it.
Now, as all beings become one with this intelligence (prajñā), so [does he attain them].
We shall now explain that.
Speech alone is one limb drawn forth from her; beyond it, the element of being is disposed as its name. Breath alone is another limb drawn forth from her.
Its odor is a further elemental constituent established therein;
the eye alone is one limb drawn out from it,
and its visible form is a further elemental constituent established therein.
The ear alone is one limb drawn out from her; sound is the elemental constituent corresponding to it from beyond. The tongue alone is one limb drawn out from her.
Beyond that, the elemental constituent of the essence of food is assigned to her.
Her two hands alone are one limb raised up;
beyond those, the elemental constituent of action is assigned to them.
The body alone is one limb of hers that has been lifted up;
beyond it, the elemental constituents (bhūtamātrā) are assigned as its pleasure and pain.
The generative organ alone is another limb of hers that has been lifted up.
Of that [body], joy, pleasure, and procreation are the elemental constituents (bhūtamātrā) established beyond [the feet].
The feet alone are one limb raised up from it;
of those two, movement is the elemental constituent established beyond them.
The mind alone is one limb drawn out from this [body];
for it, thought and desires are the corresponding elements of being established beyond it.
Having mounted speech by means of wisdom, one attains all names through speech;
having mounted the vital breath by means of wisdom, one attains all odors through the vital breath;
having mounted the eye by means of wisdom, one attains all forms through the eye.
Having mounted the ear by means of wisdom, one perceives all sounds through the ear; having mounted the tongue by means of wisdom, one perceives all tastes through the tongue;
having mounted the two hands by means of wisdom, one performs all actions with the two hands.

Having mounted the body by means of wisdom, one experiences pleasure and pain through the body; having mounted the generative organ by means of wisdom, one experiences bliss, sexual delight, and procreation through the generative organ; having mounted the feet by means of wisdom, one experiences all movements through the feet.
Having mounted the mind with wisdom, one attains all things that are to be meditated upon through the mind;
for speech devoid of wisdom cannot designate anything at all,
yet one says, "My mind was elsewhere."
"I did not perceive this name"—
for indeed, a vital breath devoid of intelligence could not perceive any scent at all;
he says, "My mind was elsewhere."
"I did not perceive this odor," he says;
for the eye, deprived of wisdom, cannot perceive any form whatsoever.
"My mind was elsewhere," he says.
"I did not perceive this form," he says;
for the ear, deprived of the mind, cannot perceive any sound at all.
He says, "My mind was elsewhere."
"I did not perceive this sound," he says;
for indeed, a tongue deprived of the mind would not perceive any taste of food.
"My mind was elsewhere," he says.
"I did not perceive this flavor of food," they said. "For indeed, hands devoid of intelligence could not perform any action; we were simply preoccupied with our minds," they replied.
"You did not perceive this action of ours.
For indeed, a body devoid of consciousness would not perceive anything at all, whether pleasure or pain;
[the person] says, "My mind was elsewhere."
"I did not perceive this as neither pleasure nor pain.
For one devoid of wisdom, Ānanda, would not perceive any bliss, delight, or procreation in the generative organ;
rather, he says, "My mind was elsewhere."

"I did not perceive this Ānanda, nor did I perceive his delight," he said. "For one whose two feet have been deprived of wisdom cannot perceive anything at all; rather, he says, 'Our minds were elsewhere.'"
"We did not understand this [truth] of yours.
For indeed, no cognition devoid of wisdom can succeed, nor can that which is to be known be known by one lacking wisdom.
"One should not seek to know speech;
one should know the speaker.
One should not seek to know smell."
One should know the smeller;
one should not seek to understand form.
One should know the seer.
"One should not seek to understand sound; one should know the hearer. One should not seek to understand the taste of food."
One should know him as the knower of the essence of food; one should not seek to know action,
but rather know him as the agent.
"One does not seek to know pleasure and pain" means one should understand the full extent of pleasure and pain. "One does not seek to know joy, delight, or procreation."
"One should know the knower of bliss, of delight, of procreation; one should desire to know the knower of this [state];
one should know the knower of this [state]."
"One should not seek to know the mind; one should know the thinker. These, indeed, are those ten elements of being with respect to wisdom.
The ten elements of wisdom are the objective counterparts;
for if the elements of matter did not exist, the elements of wisdom would not exist,
and if the elements of wisdom did not exist, the elements of matter would not exist.
For form would not be established from either one alone;
it is not that they are separate.
It is just as the rim of a chariot wheel is fixed upon the spokes.
Just as the spokes are fixed in the hub,
even so these elements (bhūtamātrā) are fixed in the elements of discernment (prajñāmātrā),
and the elements of discernment are fixed in the vital breath (prāṇa).
This very breath is the conscious self (prajñātman), infinite, undecaying, and immortal. It does not become greater by good action, nor indeed smaller by evil action.
For it is this very one that causes him to perform good action whom it wishes to lead up from these worlds;
and it is this very one that causes him to perform evil action whom it wishes to lead down.
He is the guardian of the world;
he is the sovereign of the world;
he is the lord of the world.
"One should know: 'That is my Self. One should know: 'That is my Self.'"
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka.

The Bṛhat is in the sun,
food is in the moon, and truth is in lightning.
In the thundercloud, the sound;

"In fire is the overcomer; in water is the brilliance.

In the shadow is Dvitīya;
in the echo is Asu;
in sound is Mṛtyu.
Yama is in the dream state;
Prajāpati is in the body;
Vāk is in the right eye.
In the right eye is the essence of truth.
Bālāki said: "The person who is right here in the sun, that very one I meditate upon.
Ajātaśatru said to him: "Do not make me have a conversation about him!
I meditate upon him as the Great One, clad in white raiment, the Unassailable, the Head of all beings."
He who venerates him in this way becomes pre-eminent and the head of all beings.
Bālāki said: "The person who is right here in the moon, that very one I meditate upon.
Ajātaśatru said to him: "Do not make me have a conversation about him!
I meditate upon him as the self of food."
He who venerates him in this way becomes the self of food.
Bālāki said: "The person who is right here in the lightning, him indeed I meditate upon.
Ajātaśatru said to him: "Do not make me converse about him!
I meditate upon him as the Self of truth."
He who venerates him in this way becomes the self of truth.
Bālāki said: "The person who is in the thunder—that very one I meditate upon.
Ajātaśatru said to him: "Do not make me converse about him!
I meditate upon him as the Self of sound."
He who venerates him thus becomes the self of sound.
Bālāki said: "The person who is right here in the wind—that is the one I meditate upon.
Ajātaśatru said to him: "Do not talk to me about him!
I meditate upon him as Indra Vaikuṇṭha, the unconquered army."
He who venerates him thus indeed becomes victorious, unconquerable, and a vanquisher of his enemies.
Bālāki said: "I meditate upon him who is this person in the ether.
Ajātaśatru said to him: "Do not talk to me about him!
I meditate upon him as Brahman, the Full, which does not move."
He who venerates him in this way is filled with offspring, cattle, fame, spiritual splendor, and the heavenly world; he reaches a full span of life.
Bālāki said: "The person who is here in the fire—that very one I meditate upon.
Ajātaśatru said to him: "Do not make me have a conversation about him!
I meditate upon him rather as 'the overcomer of armies' (viṣāsahiḥ)."
He who venerates him in this way indeed becomes a subduer among others.
Bālāki said: "The person who is just this one in the water, him indeed I meditate upon.
Ajātaśatru said to him: "Do not make me have a conversation about him!
I meditate upon him as the self of splendor (tejas)."
He who venerates him thus becomes the self of splendor.
This is with respect to the deities;
now, with respect to the self.
Bālāki said: "The person who is here in the mirror—that very one I worship.

Whoever worships this in such a manner, a worthy son is born to him in his offspring, and not one who is unworthy.
Bālāki said: "The person who is here in the shadow—that very one I meditate upon.
Ajātaśatru said to him: "Do not make me converse about him!
I meditate upon him as the 'Inseparable Companion' (Anapaga), the second."
He who venerates him in this way finds a companion; he becomes possessed of a companion.
Bālāki said: "The person who is here in an echo—that very one I meditate upon.
Ajātaśatru said to him: "Do not talk to me about him!

He who meditates upon this in this way does not fall into confusion before his time.
Bālāki said: "The person who is here in sound—that very one I meditate upon.
Ajātaśatru said to him: "Do not make me converse about him!

He who meditates upon him in this way does not pass away before his time.
Bālāki said: "That by which this person, when asleep, wanders about in dreams—that indeed I worship.

Whoever venerates him in this way—for him all this is indeed brought into subjection for his preeminence.
Bālāki said: "The person who is right here in the body, him indeed I meditate upon. Ajātaśatru said to him: "Do not talk to me about him! I meditate upon him as Prajāpati."
He who meditates upon this in this way is procreated with offspring, cattle, fame, and the splendor of sacred knowledge; he attains the heavenly world and reaches a full span of life.
Bālāki said: "The person who is right here in the right eye—that is the one I venerate.
Ajātaśatru said to him: "Do not talk to me about him!

He who venerates him in this way becomes the self of all these.

He who venerates him in this way becomes the self of all these.

the channels called *hitā* extend from the heart toward the pericardium; they are as fine as a hair split a thousandfold.

when one is asleep and does not perceive any dream, one exists within them at that time.

speech enters into it together with all names,

the mind merges with all thoughts.
When he awakens, [he emerges from that state].

Just as when a fire blazes, sparks fly out in all directions, even so from this Self the vital breaths (prāṇas) go forth each to its own abode; from the vital breaths the gods [go forth], and from the gods the worlds. This very vital breath is the conscious self (prajñātman); it has entered this body as the self, down to the hairs and down to the nails.
Just as a razor placed in a razor-case, or as the all-sustainer [the earth] in its abode, even so this conscious self has entered this body as its self, down to the very hairs and the nails.
These selves settle down around this self, just as one's own subjects surround their lord.
Just as the lord enjoys his own subjects, or as the subjects serve the lord.
In this very way, this Self consisting of wisdom enjoys by means of these selves;
in this very way, these selves enjoy this Self.
Indeed, for as long as Indra did not recognize this Self, for that long the Asuras overcame him.
When he understood this, then, having slain the Asuras and conquered them, he attained preeminence, sovereignty, and lordship over all the gods.
In exactly the same way, one who knows this, having cast off all evils, attains preeminence, sovereignty, and lordship over all beings—
yea, one who knows this, yea, one who knows this.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka.

This very chariot drawn by horses, with its team of side-horses, joined together by mind, speech, and vital breath, leads one to the heavenly world.

This very point is expressed by a *ṛc*: "Do not [give us] to the thieves who, dwelling in the place of the oppressor, are enemies who greedily covet our food."
