If he should speak either when instigated by another or for his own purpose, while speaking he should know: "The Saṃhitā has gone to heaven for the sake of speaking to the learned gods; it will come back in this way.
By means of this subsequent [knowledge], it indeed becomes so.
"The mother is the prior form, the father is the subsequent form, and the offspring is their union," says Bhārgava.
All this has been declared as one alone:
for indeed, all this—the mother, the father, and the offspring—is one.
This is the Aditi-saṃhitā. Indeed, Aditi is all this—whatever exists here as the universe.
This very thing is expressed by a Ṛgvedic verse: "Aditi is the sky, Aditi is the intermediate space; Aditi is the mother, she is the father, she is the son."
The All-Gods are Aditi, the five peoples are Aditi; Aditi is what has been born, and Aditi is what is yet to be born.
He who thus knows this Saṃhitā is united with offspring, cattle, fame, spiritual splendor, and the heavenly world; he attains a full lifespan.
"The wife is the prior form, the husband is the subsequent form; the son is the conjunction, the seed is the union, and procreation is the joining"—thus said Śākalya the Elder.
This is the *Prajāpati-saṃhitā*.
He who knows this *saṃhitā* is joined with offspring, cattle, fame, spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and the heavenly world; he reaches a full span of life.
"Wisdom is the prior form, faith is the subsequent form; action is the connection and truth is the joining," says Kāśyapa.
This is that connection with truth.
Regarding this, they say: "The gods are those who are joined with truth."
He who thus knows this Saṃhitā is united with offspring, cattle, fame, spiritual luster, and the heavenly world; he reaches a full lifespan.
"Speech is the *saṃhitā*," says Pañcālacaṇḍa.
"For by speech the Vedas are joined together; by speech the meters are joined; by speech they form alliances.
Therefore, whenever one studies this or speaks it, at that time the vital breath (*prāṇa*) resides in speech."
Then speech swallows breath;
and when one sleeps or becomes silent, then breath contains speech, and breath swallows speech. These two swallow each other.
This very thing has been declared by a Ṛgvedic verse: "The single bird entered the ocean."
He gazes upon this entire world;
I beheld him from nearby with a simple mind.
The mother licks him, and he licks the mother.
Thus:
Speech is indeed the mother, and breath is the calf.
He who knows this connection (*saṃhitā*) is united with offspring, cattle, fame, spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and the heavenly world; he reaches a full lifespan.
"Tārkṣya says that the *saṃhitā* is joined together by means of the form of the *Bṛhat* and the *Rathaṃtara*.
Speech is indeed the form of the *Rathaṃtara*, and breath is the form of the *Bṛhat*.
Indeed, the *saṃhitā* is joined together by both: by speech and by breath."
Regarding this very Upaniṣad, Tārkṣya used to say: "One should guard cows for a year.
He who knows this Saṃhitā in this way becomes united with offspring, cattle, fame, spiritual luster, and the heavenly world; he reaches a full lifespan.
"Motion is the prior form, cessation is the subsequent form, and stability is the conjunction (saṃhitā)," said Ārtabhāga Jāratkārava.

In this very conjunction, the destructions, moments, units of time (kāṣṭhā), divisions (kalā), instants (kṣaṇa), hours (muhūrta), days and nights, half-months, months, seasons, and years are joined together.
This is that conjunction; it joins these temporal divisions together.
Time joins together the cessation of movement and stability;
by means of the cessation of movement and stability, all this is joined together.
Thus [is explained] with reference to the deities.
Now, with reference to the self: the past is the prior form, the future is the subsequent form; that which exists between them is the *saṃhitā*, the junction of time.
This very point is expressed by a Ṛgvedic verse: "Great is that secret name, touched by many, by which they generated the past and by which they generated the future.
That ancient light which was born—into it, his beloved ones, the five [classes of beings], have entered together."
Thus it is said.
He who knows this *saṃhitā* in this manner is united with offspring, cattle, fame, Vedic splendor, and the heavenly world; he reaches a full span of life.
Now, therefore, follows the teaching of Vāliśikhāyani.
"There are these five great elements," so said Vāliśikhāyani; namely, earth, wind, space, water, and light. These exist joined together with one another.
Now, those other minor things which are joined together by the great elements—this is the "all-encompassing conjunction" (*sarva-vibhūta-saṃhitā*).
He who knows this conjunction in this way is joined with offspring, cattle, fame, spiritual luster, and the heavenly world; he reaches a full span of life.
"Every speech is Brahman," so indeed said Lauhikya;
"whatever sounds there may be, one should know them as speech alone.
Regarding this, a seer also said: "I move together with the Rudras and the Vasus."
This very speech becomes all sounds.
He who knows this *saṃhitā* thus is joined with offspring, cattle, fame, spiritual luster, and the heavenly world; he reaches a full lifespan.

And just as this Brahman becomes capable of assuming any form at will and moving according to its will, even so does he become capable of assuming any form at will and moving according to his will among all beings.
Whoever knows thus, whoever knows thus.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka.

"The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the family pillar," so said the elder Śākalya. "Just as all other beams are supported within the main pillar of a house, even so the entire self (*ātman*) is supported within this vital breath.

Of that self, the vital breath has the form of *ūṣman* (the sibilants); the bones have the form of *sparśa* (the stops); the marrow has the form of *svara* (the vowels); and flesh and blood—this fourth thing—have the form of the *antasthā* (semivowels)."
"But this has been declared as only a triad," so said Hvasra Māṇḍūkeya.
Of this very triad, there are three hundred and sixty joints; these amount to three hundred and twenty-seven. Indeed, there are three hundred and twenty days and nights in a year.
That [self] attains the days and nights of the year.
This very self is equal in measure to the year; it consists of sight, it consists of hearing, it consists of the meters, it consists of mind, and it consists of speech.
He who knows this self—equal in measure to the year, consisting of sight, hearing, the meters, mind, and speech—attains union with the year, residence in the same world, and identity of form.
He attains the state of being eaten by the assembly;
he becomes possessed of sons and cattle, and reaches a full lifespan—he who, being a descendant of Aruṇi, has performed this sacrifice for the gods.
Now, according to Kauṣṭharavya,
there are three hundred and sixty syllables and three hundred and sixty *ūṣman* sounds.
There are three hundred and sixty joints;
those syllables we have spoken of are the days,
and those *ūṣman* sounds are the nights.

"The joints we have spoken of as those of days and nights—those are the joints with respect to the deities. Now, with respect to the self: "Those syllables which we spoke of with respect to the deities are the bones with respect to the self."

That which we have called the presiding deity of heat is, with respect to the self, the marrow. This marrow is indeed the very breath; it is semen. For there is no accomplishment of semen apart from breath.
If semen were emitted without breath, it would putrefy and could not come into being.
Those joints which we have described with reference to the deities are the joints with reference to the self (adhyātma).
Of this [body], there are five hundred joints in the bones; thus, including the joints of the limbs, there are eight thousand.
There are five hundred joints in the bones, and including the joints of the limbs, that becomes eight thousand.
Eighty thousand Bṛhatī verses the Vārkalins accomplish day after day.
This is that measurement of the day, consisting of sight, consisting of hearing, consisting of the meters, consisting of mind, and consisting of speech—the self.

He who thus knows this measurement of the day as the self consisting of sight, hearing, the meters, mind, and speech, attains union with the days, residence in the same world, similarity of form, and participation in the same food.
He enjoys [these benefits]: he becomes possessed of sons and cattle, and he reaches a full lifespan.

The Vāstya-s say there are four persons: the person who is the body (*śarīrapuruṣa*), the person who is the meters (*chandaḥpuruṣa*), the person who is the Vedas (*vedapuruṣa*), and the Great Person (*mahāpuruṣa*).

Regarding what I called "the person who is the body"—that which is this divine self (*daivika ātmā*)—its essence (*rasa*) is this bodiless conscious self (*prajñātman*). Regarding what we called "the person who is the meters," it is simply the collection of syllables (*akṣarasamāmnāya*).
Its form is the *rasa* (essence).
That which we called the "Veda-Person" (*vedapuruṣa*)—by whom the gods [know] the Rigveda, the Yajurveda, and the Sāmaveda—that is the *brahmarasa* (the essence of Brahman) of this [Veda-Person].
Therefore, one should appoint as the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) the Brahman-priest who is most proficient in the Veda (*brahmiṣṭha*), who knows the secret core (*ulbaṇa*) of the sacrifice.
That which we have called the "Great Person" (mahāpuruṣa) has the year as its body, and the sun is its essence.
One should know that this bodiless conscious self (prajñātmā) and that sun are one and the same. This very truth is declared by a Ṛgvedic verse:
The brilliant array of the gods has risen—the eye of Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni.
Sūrya, the soul of all that moves and stands, has filled the heaven, the earth, and the mid-region.

"Thus," he said, "I consider this very *saṃhitā*— as it is being joined— to be the science of knowledge (*anuvidyā*)," so said Vātsya. Indeed, the Bahvṛcas investigate this very [Self] in the Great Hymn (*mahaduktha*), the Adhvaryus in the Fire-ritual (*agni*), and the Chandogas in the Mahāvrata.
In this [earth], they meditate upon him as the intermediate space; in the sky, him; in fire, him; in wind, him; in the moon, him; in the stars, him;
in the waters, him; in the plants, him; in all beings, him; in the imperishable syllables (akṣara), them—they meditate upon him alone as Brahman.
This very thing has been declared by a Ṛg-verse:
Beholding the higher light beyond the darkness,
we have gone up to Sūrya, the god among gods, the supreme light.

Thus, this very Self is the harmony of the syllables, consisting of sight, hearing, the meters, mind, and speech. Whoever praises this Self— the harmony of the syllables consisting of sight, hearing, the meters, mind, and speech— to another person, his Vedas become like a milked-out cow.
One has no share in speech, nor does one have a share in that which is not spoken;
this very point is declared by a Ṛgvedic verse:
He who has abandoned a companion who knows the truth—of him there is no share even in speech;
for what he hears, he hears in vain, since he does not know the path of righteous action.

Thus he says: "There is no part of speech that has not been spoken by him. Therefore, one should not recite this day for another; one should not pile the fire-altar, nor should one chant the Mahāvrata hymn, lest one should be deprived even of oneself.
We have said that this bodiless self consisting of intelligence and that [self] in the sun are one; these two are seen separately only where they appear distinct.
The sun appears like the moon and its rays do not manifest;
the sky becomes red like madder;
and the anus becomes distended.
One should know that his self has departed and he will not live much longer;
whatever he considers to be his duty, let him do that.
Furthermore, if he should see himself in a mirror or in water with a slanted head or no head at all, or if he should not see himself at all.
One should understand that case in exactly the same way.
Furthermore, if the shadow has gaps or does not have gaps, one should understand that case in exactly the same way.
Moreover, if the sun should appear as if with gaps, like the hub of a chariot wheel, one should understand that case in exactly the same way.
Furthermore, if fire should appear as if blue— like the neck of a peacock— or if one should see rays of light within a great cloud;
or if one should see lightning in a cloudless sky, or see it within a cloud— one should know that this too is exactly like that.

Moreover, if one were to close one's eyes and look on with indifference, one would not see those [objects] there, as if they were mere cowries; one should know that even in this case it is exactly so.

Furthermore, if one were to close one's ears and listen, when one does not hear that sound which is like the roar of a blazing fire or the rattling of a chariot, one should know that even in this case it is exactly so.
Moreover, even if the two maidens are seen to be inverted like a double-tongued serpent, or if they are not seen at all—one should know it to be exactly thus:

"He who is here unheard, unthought, unknown, unseen, unpointed out, and unproclaimed, yet who is the hearer, the thinker, the knower, the seer, the pointer, and the proclaimer, the inner person within all beings—he, I know, is my Self. As he departs, he attains this bodiless, conscious Self and abandons the other, which pertains to the body.
This indeed is the secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of all speech;
for all these [other doctrines] are indeed secret doctrines of all speech.
However, they explain this one as follows.
The *sparśa* consonants are the form of the earth, the *ūṣman* sibilants are the form of the intermediate space, and the *svara* vowels are the form of heaven.
The *sparśa* consonants are the form of fire, the *ūṣman* sibilants are the form of wind, and the *svara* vowels are the form of the sun.
The *sparśa* consonants are the form of the *Ṛgveda*, the *ūṣman* sibilants are the form of the *Yajurveda*, and the *svara* vowels are the form of the *Sāmaveda*.
The consonants (*sparśa*) are the form of the *rathantara* [Sāman]; the sibilants (*ūṣman*) are the form of the *vāmadevya*; the vowels (*svara*) are the form of the *bṛhat*.

The consonants are the form of the out-breath (*prāṇa*); the sibilants are the form of the in-breath (*apāna*); the vowels are the form of the mind (*manas*). The consonants are the form of the out-breath; the sibilants are the form of the in-breath; the vowels are the form of the up-breath (*udāna*). "Vowels"—thus it is repeated for emphasis.
Indeed, he who knows thus knows all speech.
Now, this divine lute is the prototype, and that human one is its imitation.
Just as this one possesses strings and a bridge, so too does that one possess strings and a bridge.
Just as this one has a head, so too does that one have a head.
Just as her backbone is, so is his staff;
just as her belly is, so is his water-vessel;
just as she has a mouth, nostrils, and eyes, so does he have apertures.
Just as her fingers are its finger-stops and its coverings, so are the joints of that [lute];
just as her fingers are, so are its strings;
just as her tongue is, so is its sounding.
Just as are the tones of this one, so are the tones of that one.
Just as this [vīṇā] here is covered with a hairy skin, even so that one there is covered with a hairy skin.
Indeed, in former times they used to cover the vīṇās with a hairy skin.
This indeed is the divine lute.
He who thus knows this divine lute becomes one whose face is radiant with learning; his fame reaches the earth, and people desire to hear him as he speaks in assemblies.
Whatever he strives for, let that be his; wherever noble speech is uttered, there they recognize him.
Now, therefore, follows the teaching of Tāṇḍavinda:

Just as this lute, when played by an unskilled player, does not accomplish the full purpose of the lute, even so speech, when uttered by an unskilled speaker, does not accomplish the full purpose of speech.
But just as this very lute, when played by a skilled player, accomplishes the full purpose of the lute, even so speech, when uttered by a skilled speaker, accomplishes the full purpose of speech.
Regarding this very lute, Jātūkarṇya Kātyāyanīputra says that its brilliance is the *saṃhitā*.
Now, Kṛtsna Hārita used to cite the Brāhmaṇa text on this very point.

Prajāpati, having created the creatures, fell apart; he restored himself by means of the meters. Because he restored himself by means of the meters, it is therefore called *saṃhitā*. Of this very *saṃhitā*, the letter *ṇ* is strength, the letter *ṣ* is the vital breath, and the *saṃhitā* itself is the self.
Now, this modification mixed with the small [letters] consists of those *nakāras*, *romas*, and *vyañjanas*.
Whoever should have any doubt regarding this should pronounce it with the *ṇakāra*; even if one were to say "without the *ṇakāra*," he should indeed pronounce it with the *ṇakāra*.
Likewise, whoever should have any doubt regarding this should pronounce it with the *ṣakāra*; even if one were to say "without the *ṣakāra*," he should indeed pronounce it with the *ṣakāra*.

A wise man should know that these two, the letter *ṇ* and the letter *ṣ*, when joined together in the continuous recitation (*anusaṃhita*) of the *ṛc*s, bestow long life; he should know it exactly thus.
Or rather, whatever else one might study—be it the *Vāk* (Speech), the *Itihāsa-purāṇa*, or anything else that has been made sacred (*brāhmīkṛta*)—he should know that also in this very same way.

Regarding this, Hrasva Māṇḍūkeya said: "Since we study the *ṛc*s in their continuous recitation and since we teach the chapter belonging to Māṇḍūkeya, by that means the letters *ṇ* and *ṣ* have been fully attained by us."

"Now, as for the fact that we study the *ṛc*s in their continuous sequence and that we study our own sacred recitation (*svādhyāya*), by that means the letters *ṇ* and *ṣ* have been attained by us," so said the elder Śākalya. Indeed, knowing this, the descendants of Kavaṣa used to say: "For what purpose shall we sacrifice? For what purpose shall we study? For we offer breath into speech, and speech into breath;
for that which is the source is also the place of dissolution."

These Saṃhitās one should not recite to one who is not a resident pupil, nor to one who has not lived [as a student] for a year, nor to one who is not a celibate student, nor to one who does not know the Veda, nor to one with a crooked mouth; so say the teachers—so say the teachers.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka.
Oṃ! We choose that inspiration of the god Savitṛ, the nourishment which is most excellent and all-sustaining.
We meditate upon the swift power of Bhaga; we meditate upon that most excellent splendor of Savitṛ; we meditate upon the glory of the divine one.
May he inspire our thoughts.
Unassailable is the mind, swift is the eye;
Sūrya is the best among lights. O Dīkṣā, do not harm me!
Verily, he who knows the eldest and the best becomes indeed the eldest and the best among his own people.
Breath is indeed the eldest and the best. Verily, he who knows the most excellent becomes the most excellent among his own people; speech is indeed the most excellent.
He who knows the foundation (pratiṣṭhā) indeed stands firm in this world and in that world; the eye, indeed, is the foundation.
He who knows the attainment (saṃpad) truly attains his desires; the ear, indeed, is the attainment.
He who knows the abode (āyatana) becomes an abode for his own people; the mind, indeed, is the abode.
Then those deities, Hā and Mā, approached their father Prajāpati and said, "Who among us is the best?
Prajāpati replied, "He among you, upon whose departure the body is considered most wretched, he indeed is the best."
Then speech departed from him;
he remained as if mute, breathing with the breath, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, and thinking with the mind—just so.
The eye departed.
[The others said: "As if blind, not seeing, yet breathing with the breath, speaking with speech, hearing with the ear, and thinking with the mind—just so!"
The sense of hearing departed; [the others said:
"It is as if we were deaf, not hearing, yet breathing with the breath, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, and thinking with the mind."
The mind departed; [the others said:
"As if children were without mind—yet breathing with the breath, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, and hearing with the ear."
The vital breath (prāṇa) departed.
Then, just as a fine horse from the Sindhu country might pull up its tethering pegs, so did that [breath] pull up the other vital breaths.
They gathered together and said, "O Blessed One, do not depart!"
Prāṇa said: "What shall be my food? "Whatever there is, down to dogs and down to birds," they replied. He said: "And what shall be my clothing? "Water," they said.
Therefore, even one who is not going to study [the Veda] encloses this [fire-altar] with water both before and after;
for he becomes a possessor of clothing, since he is no longer naked.
Indeed, Satyakāma Jābāla, having told this to Gośruti Vaiyāghrapadya, said: "He will become a possessor of clothing."
"Even if one were to say of a withered stump, 'May its branches grow, may it put forth leaves,' [it would not happen];
but [if one says], 'O Lord of the Forest, grow with a hundred shoots; do not scratch the sky, do not harm the mid-region,' so said Yājñavalkya."

Now, if he should desire to go to the Great [Sacrifice], having been initiated for three nights, on the new moon day he should prepare a mash of all herbs mixed with curds and honey; having established the fire, swept around it, strewn grass around it, and sprinkled water around it, he should bend his right knee, place the mash in a bronze vessel to the north of the fire, offer the oblations, and pour the remnants of the offerings into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with the words, "To the eldest, to the best, svāhā!", he should pour the residue into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with the words, "To the foundation, svāhā!", he should pour the residue into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with the words, "To prosperity, svāhā!", he should pour the residue into the mash.

Having eaten it in portions with the verse "That excellent glory of Savitṛ," and having sipped water in portions with the verse "We choose that of Savitṛ," he rinses his mouth for the fourth time with the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*). Having wiped the bronze vessel, he lies down upon a skin or on a bare patch of ground.
If he should see a woman, he should know: "The rite has been successful; the rite has been successful."
Thus ends the ninth chapter of the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka.
Now, therefore, follows the internal [sacrifice];
they call it the internal *agnihotra*.
Indeed, these deities are established in the person alone: Agni in speech, Vāyu in breath, Āditya in the eye, Candramas in the mind, the quarters in the ear, and the waters in the semen.
In all these [fires], indeed, an offering is truly made for one who, knowing this, eats and drinks, and causes others to eat and drink;
he eats, he drinks, he is satisfied, and he satisfies [others].
Being satisfied, he satisfies speech;
speech, being satisfied, satisfies fire;
fire, being satisfied, satisfies the earth.
The earth is satisfied; it satisfies everything that is covered by the earth—whatever has been, whatever will be, and whatever exists.
He who, knowing this, eats and drinks, and causes others to eat and drink—he eats, he drinks, he is satisfied, and he satisfies.
Being satisfied, it satisfies the vital breath (prāṇa);
the vital breath, being satisfied, satisfies the wind (vāyu);
the wind, being satisfied, satisfies space (ākāśa).
Space is satisfied; whatever is covered by space—whether past, present, or future—it satisfies all that.
He who, knowing this, eats and drinks, and causes others to eat and drink—he eats, he drinks, he is satisfied, and he satisfies.
Being satisfied, it satisfies the eye;
the satisfied eye satisfies the sun;
the satisfied sun satisfies the heavens.
The Satisfied Sky satisfies everything that is covered by heaven—whatever has been, whatever is to be, and whatever exists.
He who, knowing this, eats and drinks, and causes others to eat and drink—he eats, he drinks, he is satisfied, and he satisfies.
When that is satisfied, it satisfies the mind; the satisfied mind satisfies the moon;
the satisfied moon satisfies the stars.
The satisfied constellations satisfy the months;
the satisfied months satisfy the half-months;
the satisfied half-months satisfy the days and nights.
When day and night are satisfied, they satisfy the seasons;
the seasons, being satisfied, satisfy the year;
the year, being satisfied, satisfies everything that is covered by the year—whatever has been, whatever is to be, and whatever is present.
He who, knowing thus, eats and drinks, and causes others to eat and drink—he eats, he drinks, he is satisfied, and he satisfies.
Being satisfied, it satisfies the ear;
the satisfied ear satisfies the quarters;
the satisfied quarters satisfy the intermediate directions.
It satisfies the intermediate directions; whatever is covered by the intermediate directions—whether present, future, or past—it satisfies all that.
He who, knowing this, eats and drinks, and causes others to eat and drink—he eats, he drinks, he is satisfied, and he satisfies others.
Being satisfied, it satisfies the semen;
the semen, being satisfied, satisfies the waters;
the waters, being satisfied, satisfy the rivers.
The rivers, being satisfied, satisfy the ocean;
the ocean, being satisfied, satisfies everything that is covered by the ocean—whatever has been, whatever will be, and whatever is present.
He who, knowing this, eats and drinks, causes others to eat and drink—he indeed eats, he drinks, he is satisfied, and he satisfies.

When he is satisfied, this very Agnihotra becomes tenfold and belongs to Vairāja. Of it, the out-breath (*prāṇa*) is the Āhavanīya fire; the in-breath (*apāna*) is the Gārhapatya fire; the diffused breath (*vyāna*) is the Anvāhāryapacana fire; the mind (*manas*) is the smoke; passion (*manyu*) is the flame; the teeth are the embers; faith (*śraddhā*) is the milk; speech (*vāk*) is the fuel; truth (*satya*) is the oblation; and the conscious self (*prajñātman*) is its essence.
Thus, this tenfold Agnihotra becomes offered as the Vairāja.
Ascended by each successive ascent, it causes [the sacrificer] to go to the heavenly world—provided he eats and drinks, and causes others to eat and drink, knowing this.
But for one who offers the Agnihotra without knowing this, it would be just as if, having removed the embers, the offering were made in ashes; such indeed would that be.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka.
Prajāpati indeed raised up this person;

he caused these deities to enter into him: Agni into the speech, Vāyu into the breath, lightning into the downward breath, Parjanya into the upward breath, Āditya into the eye, Candramas into the mind, the quarters into the ear, the earth into the body, the waters into the seed, and Indra into the strength.
He placed Manyu in the head, Īśāna in the sky, and Brahman in the self.
Just as a great jar of nectar might stand overflowing, even so did he stand.
Then these deities reflected: "What will this person do with us, or what shall we do with him?"
"Come, let us depart from this body.
So they departed.
Then this body was, as it were, empty and full of holes. Prajāpati then reflected: "It is not fit for me to remain in a state of deficiency."
"Come, let me afflict these [beings] with hunger and thirst. He afflicted them;
and being thus afflicted, finding no comfort, they entered back into this very person.
"Speech is mine"—thus Agni entered; "Breath is mine"—thus Vāyu entered;
"Exhalation is mine"—thus the lightnings entered.
"Breath is mine"—thus Parjanya entered him; "The eye is mine"—thus Āditya entered him;
"The mind is mine"—thus Candramas entered him.
"The ear is ours," [saying this] they entered the quarters;
"The body is mine," [saying this] the earth entered;
"Semen is ours," [saying this] the waters entered.
"Strength is mine"—thus Indra entered him; "Wrath is mine"—thus Īśāna entered him;
"The head is mine"—thus Space entered him.
"The Self is mine"—with this thought, Brahman entered him.
Just as a great tree, moist and with its roots well-watered, might stand firm, even so did he stand.
Then, before a year has passed, this man, while about to depart, sees the omens of the year:
the shadow becomes perforated or it does not appear at all;
or he might see mirages as if in a great cloud, or he might see lightning even when there is no cloud, or he might not see it even when there is a cloud.
As if his eyes were covered, he does not see even cowries;
as if his ears were covered, he does not hear even the sound of a drum;
he finds no delight in this world, nor does his mind find pleasure in it.
Thus end the direct perceptions.
Now, regarding dreams:
he sees a black man with black teeth who strikes him; a boar strikes him; a monkey strikes him; he strikes him;
he eats lotus stalks; having swallowed gold, he vomits it up; he holds a single *pauṇḍarīka* flower.

Facing the south, wearing a garland of *nalada* grass, he drives out a cow with her calf. If he should see anything among these— such as a pale-looking black woman with loose hair, a shaven-headed woman, an oil-anointing,
a saffron-colored garment, songs, mounting a camel, or traveling toward the southern direction— he should fast and [offer] milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and a pot-cooked oblation (*sthālīpāka*).

Having cooked [the oblation] in the milk of a cow that has a calf of the same color— though never that of a black cow— and having established the fire, swept around it, strewn grass around it, and sprinkled water around it, he bends his right knee and offers oblations of clarified butter with the dipping-spoon (sruva).
In my speech Agni is established, svāhā!
In my out-breath Vāyu is established, svāhā!
In my in-breath the lightnings are established, svāhā!
In my upward breath, Parjanya is established; svāhā! In my eye, Āditya is established; svāhā!
In my mind, Candramas is established; svāhā!
The quarters are established in my ears; svāhā!
The earth is established in my body; svāhā! The waters are established in my semen; svāhā!
In my strength, Indra is established; svāhā! In my mind, Īśāna is established; svāhā! In my head, Ākāśa is established; svāhā!
"Brahman is established in my self, svāhā!
Then, having poured the remainder of this clarified butter into the pot of cooked rice, he offers a portion of that cooked rice as an oblation.

Fire is established in my speech; speech is in the heart; the heart is in the Self. That is the truth of the gods. May I not die with unfulfilled desire; may I have food and be an eater of food—*svāhā*! Vāyu is established in my breath; breath is in the heart; the heart is in the Self. That is the truth of the gods. May I not die with unfulfilled desire; may I have food and be an eater of food—*svāhā*!

Lightning is established in my downward breath; the downward breath is in the heart; the heart is in the Self. That is the truth of the gods. May I not die with unfulfilled desire; may I have food and be an eater of food—*svāhā*!

In my *udāna* breath Parjanya is established; the *udāna* is in the heart, the heart in the self. That is the truth of the gods. May I not die with unfulfilled desire; may I be possessed of food, a consumer of food. *Svāhā!* In my eye Āditya is established; the eye is in the heart, the heart in the self. That is the truth of the gods. May I not die with unfulfilled desire; may I be possessed of food, a consumer of food. *Svāhā!* In my mind Candramas is established; the mind is in the heart, the heart in the self. That is the truth of the gods. May I not die with unfulfilled desire; may I be possessed of food, a consumer of food. *Svāhā!*

In my ear the quarters are established; the quarters are in the heart, the heart in the Self. That is the truth of the gods. May I not die with unfulfilled desire; may I be possessed of food, a consumer of food—*svāhā*! In my body the earth is established; the earth is in the heart, the heart in the Self. That is the truth of the gods. May I not die with unfulfilled desire; may I be possessed of food, a consumer of food—*svāhā*!

In my strength Indra is established; strength is in the heart, the heart in the Self. That is the truth of the gods. May I not die with unfulfilled desire; may I be possessed of food, a consumer of food—*svāhā*!

In my mind is established Īśāna; the mind is in the heart, and the heart is in the Self. That is the truth of the gods: may I not die with unfulfilled desire, but be possessed of food and a consumer of food—Svāhā!

In my head is established Ākāśa; the head is in the heart, and the heart is in the Self. That is the truth of the gods: may I not die with unfulfilled desire, but be possessed of food and a consumer of food—Svāhā!

"Brahman is established in my self; the self is in the heart, and the heart is in the self. That is the truth of the gods. May I not die with unfulfilled desire; may I possess food and be an eater of food. Svāhā!
Then, having poured the remainder of this *sthālīpāka* into his own self, he offers it as an oblation.

The stone is the Jagatī; iron is the Triṣṭubh; bronze is the Uṣṇih; lead is the Kakubh; silver is self-sovereignty; gold is the Gāyatrī; food is the Vairāja; satisfaction is the Anuṣṭubh; the firmament is sovereignty; Bṛhaspati is the Bṛhatī;
the sacred word is the Paṅkti; Prajāpati is the Atichandas; the Sāvitrī is by means of the meters of all the Vedas—by means of the meter.
May I dwell firm as a stone with the *jagatī* metre.
The person is the amulet, the breath is the thread, and food is the knot; that knot I untie, desiring food.
To Death [I offer] the Brahmin; may I reach a full lifespan. May I, long-lived and free from desire, not die; may I become possessed of food and an eater of food. *Svāhā!*

May I dwell firm as iron; by means of the Triṣṭubh metre, may the man, the amulet, the breath—svāhā! May I dwell firm as bronze; by means of the Auṣṇiha metre, may the man, the amulet, the breath—svāhā! May I dwell firm as lead; by means of the Kākubha metre, may the man, the amulet, the breath—svāhā!

May I abide firm like silver; by means of the Svarāj metre, may the person, the jewel, the breath... Svāhā! May I abide firm like gold; by means of the Gāyatrī metre, may the person, the jewel, the breath... Svāhā! May I abide firm like food; by means of the Vairāja metre, may the person, the jewel, the breath... Svāhā!
May I wear [it] firmly like satisfaction; by means of the Anuṣṭubh metre, may the Puruṣa-gem, the breath—svāhā!
May I wear [it] firmly like the vault of heaven; by means of the Sāmrājya metre, may the Puruṣa-gem, the breath—svāhā!

May I dwell firm like Bṛhaspati; by means of the Bārhata metre, may the person, the amulet, the breath... Svāhā! May I dwell firm like Brahmā; by means of the Pāṅkta metre, may the person, the amulet, the breath... Svāhā! May I dwell firm like Prajāpati; by means of the Ātichandas metre, may the person, the amulet, the breath... Svāhā!
"Like the Sāvitrī verses, may I dwell firm; by the meter of all the Vedas, by the meter, the person is the amulet, the vital breath... Svāhā!
He should give the remains of the food to his beloved wife, or to his beloved pupil, or to anyone else for whom he might have a desire.
He indeed lives for a hundred years; practicing this again and again, he truly lives, he truly lives.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka.
Om! May the great luster of an elephant and abundant vitality, which was produced from the body of Aditi, be extended for me; may all these Ādityas, in harmony with Aditi, bestow it upon me. 1.
O Jātavedas, with that great luster which is yours and has been placed [within you], with that luster, O Agni, make me full of luster. // 2 //
Whatever luster is in a man, and whatever is placed in elephants, whatever luster is in gold and in cows—may that elephant-luster be in me. (3)
Whatever glory is in dice, in gold, in cattle, and in horses; whatever glory is in the fermenting surā—may that splendor of an elephant be in me. 4.
May splendor be in me, may greatness be in me, and whatever glory belongs to the sacrifice, may Prajāpati establish that in me, as one makes heaven firm upon heaven. //5//
O Aśvins, may you anoint me with the honeyed milk of the bee;
so that I may utter speech full of sweetness among the people. 6.
Drawn forth from clarified butter, rich in honey, full of milk, the winner of wealth, the supporter, the sustainer—crushing my rivals and casting them down, ascend me for great good fortune! 7.
O Prajāpati, none other than you has encompassed all these created beings.
Whatever desire we have as we offer this oblation to you, may that be ours; may we be masters of riches. 8.
May this *sana* drive away my rivals, like Indra, the victor in battles, driving away Vṛtra;
like Agni spread in many places, it consumes the dry wood; with its sharp-jawed flame, it sweeps through us like the wind. 9.
This is the benevolent one, the follower who, like a pillar, shattered Vṛtra and his fortresses;
with him, Indra having struck down the adversaries, has brought forth the enjoyments of those who act as enemies. 10.
O Jayendra, slay the enemies, O hero; strike down the Dasyus as one cleaves Vṛtra with the thunderbolt.
Drive away the curses like a flood; slay the rivals as an axe fells the woods. 11.
Cut them down from the middle; cut them down from above; cut them down from behind; O hero, cut them down!
O Maghavan, let the Maruts follow the enemies driven away by you, O hero, as they perish. 12.
The Maruts, swelling you with their Rudra-weapons and regarding you as Indra, have taken pleasure in you;
may the well-winged Kaṅkas seize them, and may the fanged one exult in his growths.
O Maghavan Indra, let the crushing blows of the one who attacks the supreme Brahman fall in every direction.
Let him have neither a kinsman nor a support; striking one another down, they go to their death. 14.
O glorious Agni, bestow glory upon him; bring here the honor-giving worship associated with Indra.
May this one be the supreme head, most exalted, and possess great luster; may he be the highest in renown among his kinsmen. 15.
Beholding the auspicious, they approached; from that the seers who have found the light attained consecration (*dīkṣā*).
From that, sovereignty, strength, and vigor were born; may the gods bow down in unison to this for him. 16.

The Ordainer, the Disposer, the supreme beholder, Prajāpati, Parameṣṭhin, the resplendent—these have declared to me the hymns, the meters, and the invocations; let the kingdom bow down completely unto him. 17.
Turn back toward it; attend upon Agni. May he be our sovereign ruler. Take hold of his wisdom; all of you shall live following after him. 18.
Long ago you were born as Alarda, before the sun and before the dawn;
I know you as the destroyer of rivals, the one who crushes those who obstruct. 19.
One shall not die prematurely; he shall cross over his enemy, his speech shall be effective, and he shall prevail over hostile armies.
They say that the one who bears the *irāmaṇi* amulet made of *bilva* wood brings death upon his enemy. (20)
He who bears the *rāmaṇi* staff made of *bilva* wood does not consume the sin of a curse, nor does the divine Varuṇa strike him in his fear; the wrathful fury of the gods does not overcome him. (21)
The Jātavedas does not harm its skin, nor does it eat its flesh, nor does it destroy those [limbs].
He who bears this sacrificial ladle made of Bilva wood attains a hundred-year lifespan and reaches old age in this world. 22.

The offspring of one who wears this *irāmaṇi* amulet made of *bilva* wood does not become defective at birth; he does not become a mountain-dweller [or a beast], nor does he engage in sinful deeds. No other discord arises among his families. 23.
Neither revilers nor those who speak ill enter his house; misfortune finds no dwelling in him who bears this *irāmaṇi* amulet made of bilva wood. (24)

Neither a *rakṣas*, nor a *piśāca*, nor a *jambhaka*, nor an *asura*, nor a *yakṣa* harms him who carries this *irāmaṇī* amulet made of *bilva* wood; moreover, no woman afflicted by *sūtikā* (childbirth fever) is born in his families. //25//
Neither tiger, nor wolf, nor leopard, nor any beast of prey shall harm him;
nor does fear from an enraged elephant come upon him who wears this amulet made of bilva wood.
Neither a snake nor a viper harms him, nor a scorpion, nor a cross-lined adder; neither does the black serpent strike him who wears the *irāmaṇi* amulet made of bilva wood. (27)
Varuṇa does not strike down this heedless man, nor does the makara, nor the grāha, nor the śiṃśumāra;
he who wears the bilva amulet made of wood from the riverbank brings him auspiciousness from both the near and the far shore. 28.
They say his enemy is joined with destruction; like a flower cut from its stalk, he is severed along with his support.
Like a flood, drive away the curses and the rivals.
He who wears an *irāmaṇi* amulet made of *bilva* wood. // 29 //
This amulet, a protective talisman, is bound upon Jambu for the sake of life;
by means of it, Indra slew Vṛtra, together with the wise seer. (30)
Overpower the enemies of Indra; overpower the adversaries; overpower those who attack us.
Like an elephant with its two forefeet, trample down those who seek to fight us. 31.
This male amulet made of *bilva* wood has arrived, the destroyer of rivals;
the wise, all-heroic ones behold it so that they may overcome their enemies in battle. (32)
"O Aśvins, may you fasten the cord of truth upon my amulet.
You are made of Bilva wood and possess a thousandfold power; may I, your wearer, suffer no harm. (33)
Drawn from ghee, rich in honey, full of milk, the winner of wealth, the supporter, the sustainer—crushing my rivals and casting them down, ascend me for great good fortune! 34.
O Prajāpati, none other than you has encompassed all these created beings.
Whatever desire we offer to you with this oblation, may that be ours; may we be masters of riches. 35.
"Thus you have commanded; you are indeed great"—these are five [verses].
Now, therefore, follows the ritual for the amulet (*maṇikalpa*).

One desiring prosperity, having fasted for three nights, should extract a fragment from the tusks of a living elephant; then, having established the fire, swept around it, strewn grass around it, and sprinkled water around it, he should bend his right knee and place the amulet in a bronze vessel to the north of the fire.

Having performed the oblations, he should pour the remnants into the gem with these eight verses, one for each, beginning with "The splendor of an elephant" (*hastivarcasam*). After letting it soak in honey and clarified butter for seven nights, he should fasten it on for three nights or for one night with this verse: "Drawn out from the ghee" (*ghṛtād ulluptaḥ*).

From that same [gem], he should fasten another for three nights or for one night after letting it soak in meat-rice for six days—a gem from the tip of a heart-spike, or from the tip of a goad, or from the tip of a pestle, or a gem of the heartwood of *khadira*—with the following six verses.
Therefore, subsequently, one should soak a gem from the tip of a bull's horn in ghee-rice for three nights or for one night, and then tie it on;
therefore, subsequently, one should soak a castor-seed gem in sesame-rice for three nights or for one night, and then tie it on;

therefore, subsequently, one should soak a gem from the Bilva tree in honey and clarified butter for seven nights, and then tie it on for three nights or for one night with this verse: "Drawn out from the clarified butter... (RV 10.97.8).

For this very reason, the subsequent [instruction] is as follows: having soaked the milk-extract of the great *vara* tree in mung-bean rice for three nights or for one night, one should tie it on if one has the capacity;
or, being seated either in the shadow of an elephant or upon a tiger skin, one should offer the oblation—whether seated or indeed even while standing, one should offer the oblation.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka.
Now, therefore, when the body has been purified by dispassion, one should be devoted to the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña).
Thus, one conquers rebirth.
Now, indeed, it is said: "The Self must be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon."
"Māṇḍūkeya says that they desire to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, through celibacy, austerity, faith, sacrifice, and fasting.
Therefore, one who knows thus, having become calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and filled with faith, should see the Self in the very Self; so says Māṇḍavya.

This person consisting of consciousness among the vital breaths—he is this Self described as 'not this, not this. He is ungraspable, for he is not grasped. [He is] this Brahman, this Kṣatra, these gods, these Vedas, these worlds, all these beings, and this—"
"All this is this Self;
that is what 'That thou art' means—it is to be realized through the Self as 'I am Brahman.
This very Brahman is without prior, without posterior, without inner, without outer; this Self is Brahman, the experiencer of all"—this is the instruction, said Yājñavalkya.

"One should not speak this to one who is not a son or to one who is not a pupil. This is the instruction: "One might give away this earth, encompassed by waters and filled with wealth, yet this [teaching] is more than that; this indeed is more than that. One must not speak this Upaniṣad, the head of the Veda, in any manner whatsoever to an unworthy person.
This very point has been declared by a Ṛgvedic verse:
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter of the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka.

"He who does not study the head of the *ṛcs*, the supreme limb of the *yajus* formulas, the crest of the *sāmans*, and the very crown of the *atharvans*— him they call ignorant, even though he has studied the Veda."
Having severed the head, he makes a headless trunk (kabandha).
"This man is like a wooden post; he is merely a bearer of burdens, for having studied the Veda, he does not understand its meaning.
He who knows the meaning attains all that is auspicious."
He whose evil has been shaken off by knowledge goes to the heavenly realm.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka.
Now, the lineage: Om, salutation to Brahman, salutation to the teachers! We have studied this from Śāṅkhāyana, who was called Guṇa.
Guṇākhya Śāṅkhāyana [received it] from Kahoḷa Kauṣītaki;
Kahoḷa Kauṣītaki from Uddālaka Āruṇi;
Uddālaka Āruṇi from Priyavrata Saumāpi.
Priyavrata was the son of Saumāpi; Somapi was the son of Somapa; Somapa was the son of Sauma Prātiveśya; and Sauma Prātiveśya was the son of Prativeśya.
Prativeśya from Bṛhaddiva;
Bṛhaddiva from Sumnayu; Sumnayu from Uddālaka.
Uddālaka from Viśvamanas;
Viśvamanas from Vyaśva;
Vyaśva from Sākamaśva.
Sākamaśva from Devarāta;
Devarāta from Viśvāmitra;
Viśvāmitra from Indra.
Indra [is the son] of Prajāpati;
Prajāpati [is the son] of Brahmā;
Brahmā is the Self-Existent (Svayaṃbhū).
Homage to Brahmā, homage to Brahmā!
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka.
Thus ends the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka.
